sections.title: Description and History
sections.summary: Chapter 10 heading for the description and history of the reinforced soil technologies covered: reinforced embankments over soft soils, reinforced soil (MSE) walls, reinforced soil slopes and soil nail walls, plus related technologies, glossary and primary references (pp. 10-1 to 10-6).
sections.body: Section 1.0 (p. 10-1) is the heading for the chapter's introduction. It is subdivided into an introduction (1.1), a description and historical overview of each technology with the focus and scope of the chapter (1.2), a glossary of terms and acronyms (1.3) and the primary FHWA and AASHTO references where detailed guidance is given (1.4).
key_points: The chapter covers four principal reinforced soil technologies used in highway works plus related technologies.
Guidance is abridged; detailed design guidance is in other FHWA GECs and reference manuals.
sections.applicability: Use as the entry point for the overview of reinforced soil technologies in GEC 13 Volume II Chapter 10.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces the soil reinforcement technologies addressed in Chapter 10: reinforced embankments over soft soils, reinforced soil retaining walls, reinforced soil slopes and soil nail walls, the principal reinforced soil technologies used in highway works; related technologies are described at the end of the chapter (p. 10-1).
sections.body: Several soil reinforcement technologies are addressed within the chapter (p. 10-1): reinforced embankments over soft soils; reinforced soil retaining walls; reinforced soil slopes; and soil nail walls. These are the principal reinforced soil technologies used in highway works. Related technologies are listed and described at the end of the chapter (Section 6.0).
key_points: Four technologies: reinforced embankments over soft soils, reinforced soil retaining walls, reinforced soil slopes, soil nail walls.
Related technologies are covered in Section 6.0.
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying which reinforced soil technology of Chapter 10 fits a highway application.

sections.title: Description, Historical Overview, Focus, and Scope
sections.summary: Historical overview of soil reinforcement from straw-reinforced adobe and branch-reinforced dikes to modern steel (strip, bar mat, welded or woven wire mesh) and geosynthetic (geotextile, geogrid, geocomposite, geostrip; PET, HDPE, PP) reinforcements, and the chapter's abridged scope (p. 10-1).
sections.body: Inclusions have been used since prehistoric times to improve soil (p. 10-1): straw in adobe bricks, sticks and branches in mud dwellings, dikes of earth and tree branches used for at least 1,000 years, sticks used by 17th- and 18th-century settlers to reinforce mud dikes, and wooden pegs for erosion and landslide control. Soil reinforcing can also be achieved by plant roots. Modern applications use steel or geosynthetic reinforcements. Steel reinforcements are generally galvanized and in strip, bar mat, welded wire mesh (WWM) or woven wire mesh form. Polymeric reinforcements are geotextile, geogrid, geocomposite or geostrip, generally polyester (PET), high density polyethylene (HDPE) or polypropylene (PP) based. PET fiber geogrids and geostrips are coated with acrylic, polyvinyl chloride (PVC) or polyethylene (PE) to hold the fibers in grid or strip form and to protect them during installation. The chapter presents abridged guidance on construction and materials, design, specifications, quality assurance and costs, because detailed guidance is provided in other FHWA Geotechnical Engineering Circulars (GECs) and reference manuals (Section 1.4).
key_points: Steel reinforcements: generally galvanized; strip, bar mat, welded wire mesh or woven wire mesh.
Geosynthetic reinforcements: geotextile, geogrid, geocomposite or geostrip; PET, HDPE or PP based.
PET geogrids and geostrips are coated with acrylic, PVC or PE for form and installation protection.
Chapter guidance is an overview; detailed guidance is in the GECs listed in Section 1.4.
sections.applicability: Background for selecting reinforcement types and for locating detailed FHWA guidance on reinforced soil.

sections.title: Reinforced Embankments
sections.summary: Embankments over soft soils (EOSS) can fail by rotational instability or lateral spreading; high-strength geotextile or geogrid layers at the embankment-foundation interface increase resistance, acting like a flexible mat foundation. Detailed guidance is in FHWA (2008a) (p. 10-2).
sections.body: Embankments over soft soils (EOSS) have several potential failure modes (p. 10-2). Rotational slope stability failure through the embankment and foundation can occur; reinforcement placed at the embankment-to-foundation interface can increase the resistance and stabilize the structure. Embankments on soft foundations also tend to spread laterally because of horizontal earth pressures within the embankment, which cause horizontal shear stresses at its base that the foundation soil must resist; if it cannot, failure can result. Properly designed horizontal layers of high-strength geotextile or geogrid can increase lateral sliding stability and prevent such failures. Fundamentally, the reinforced soil at the base of the embankment is equivalent to a flexible mat foundation, preventing failure through the embankment and spreading the load over its full width. Reinforcement is one of several technologies for embankments over soft soils, and other foundation treatment alternatives should be considered in preliminary design (see other chapters and GeoTechTools). The engineering of reinforced embankments over soft soils is very well established; detailed FHWA guidance is FHWA (2008a), with training in NHI courses #132013A and #132013D.
key_points: Failure modes include rotational stability through embankment and foundation and lateral spreading.
Basal geotextile or geogrid acts like a flexible mat foundation.
Detailed guidance: FHWA (2008a) Geosynthetic Design and Construction Guidelines.
sections.applicability: Applies to embankments, dikes and levees built over soft foundation soils where basal reinforcement is considered.

sections.title: Reinforced Soil Walls
sections.summary: History of MSE walls: steel-strip reinforced walls pioneered in the early 1960s, first U.S. use in 1972; more than 9,000,000 sq ft of precast-faced MSE walls built per year on average, tallest wall 150 ft; detailed guidance in GEC 11 and AASHTO (2014) (pp. 10-2 to 10-3).
sections.body: Modern soil reinforcement for retaining walls was pioneered by a French architect and engineer in the early 1960s, leading to a proprietary system with steel strip reinforcements placed horizontally in multiple, equally spaced layers attached to metallic and later precast concrete facing panels (p. 10-2). The first such wall in the United States was built in 1972 on a state highway. More than 9,000,000 square feet of MSE retaining walls with precast facing are estimated to be built on average every year (GEC 11); the tallest wall constructed is 150 feet high. Many proprietary and nonproprietary systems followed. Geotextile use in walls followed its benefit in embankments over weak soils: the first geotextile-reinforced wall was built in 1971 (Puig et al. 1977) and the first in the U.S. in 1974 (USDA 1977) (p. 10-3). Geogrids were developed around 1980, first used in earth reinforcement in 1981, and in extensive use from about 1983. More than 3,000,000 square feet of modular block wall (MBW) faced, geosynthetic reinforced MSE walls are estimated to be built yearly for transportation applications (GEC 11). MSE wall engineering is very well established; detailed FHWA guidance is GEC 11 and AASHTO (2014), with training in NHI courses #132042, #132043 and #132080.
key_points: First U.S. steel-strip MSE wall: 1972; tallest U.S. wall: 150 ft.
>9,000,000 sq ft/yr of precast-faced MSE walls; >3,000,000 sq ft/yr of MBW-faced geosynthetic MSE walls (GEC 11).
First geotextile wall 1971 (Puig et al. 1977); first U.S. 1974 (USDA 1977); geogrids from about 1980.
Detailed guidance: GEC 11 and AASHTO (2014).
sections.applicability: Background on MSE (reinforced soil) retaining walls and the FHWA/AASHTO documents that govern their design.

sections.title: Reinforced Soil Slopes
sections.summary: Reinforced soil slopes (RSS) use multiple horizontal reinforcement layers between compacted lifts in a constructed earth slope, with a facing (often vegetated) to prevent erosion; tallest U.S. RSS 141 ft; about 150 RSS projects a year by 2009; guidance in GEC 11 (p. 10-3).
sections.body: Reinforced soil slopes, as with MSE walls, consist of multiply spaced, horizontal reinforcement layers placed between compacted soil lifts, but in a constructed earth slope (p. 10-3). The reinforcements extend to the face of the slope and are attached to a facing system, often vegetated, to prevent erosion of the face. The first reported use of reinforced steepened slopes (RSS) is believed to be an ancient defensive wall embankment. The tallest successfully designed, constructed and in-service RSS structure in the United States to date is 141 feet high. Use of RSS has expanded dramatically; as of 2009 more than about 150 RSS projects were being constructed yearly on transportation projects, and the number is growing. Geosynthetic and steel WWM reinforcements are used. The engineering of reinforced soil slopes is very well established; detailed FHWA guidance is GEC 11, with training on RSS on firm foundations in NHI courses #132042 and #132043.
key_points: Tallest in-service U.S. RSS: 141 ft.
About 150 RSS transportation projects per year as of 2009.
Reinforcements: geosynthetics and steel welded wire mesh; facing often vegetated.
Detailed guidance: GEC 11.
sections.applicability: Background on reinforced soil slopes built on firm foundations in transportation works.

sections.title: Soil Nail Walls
sections.summary: History of soil nail walls: an early 1976 application supported a 45-ft deep excavation in about half the time and about 85 percent of the cost of conventional support; FHWA funded a 40-ft prototype demonstration wall in 1984; detailed guidance in GEC 7 (pp. 10-3 to 10-4).
sections.body: One of the first U.S. applications was in 1976, when soil nails supported a 45-foot deep excavation for a hospital expansion; the system was completed in nearly half the time and at about 85 percent of the cost of conventional excavation-support systems (FHWA 1998) (pp. 10-3 to 10-4). In 1984 FHWA funded a demonstration project for a prototype 40-foot high soil nail wall (Nicholson 1986). Use of soil nail walls for roadway projects has since increased greatly because of technical feasibility and cost-competitiveness. For certain subsurface and project conditions soil nailing is more advantageous than other top-down earth retaining systems because the construction equipment is smaller and it provides greater structural redundancy. Easements tend to be smaller because soil nails are shorter than ground anchors for the same wall height, and the number of qualified soil-nail specialty contractors has grown (GEC 7). The engineering of soil nail walls is very well established; detailed FHWA guidance is GEC 7, with training in NHI course #132085.
key_points: 1976: 45-ft deep excavation, about half the time and about 85% of the cost of conventional support (FHWA 1998).
1984: FHWA prototype 40-ft high demonstration wall (Nicholson 1986).
Smaller equipment, greater redundancy and smaller easements than anchored systems.
Detailed guidance: GEC 7.
sections.applicability: Background on soil nail walls for top-down excavation support in roadway work.

sections.title: Related Technologies
sections.summary: Notes that several technologies are related to or extend the four primary reinforcement applications (embankments over soft soils, MSE walls, reinforced soil slopes and soil nail walls); they are listed and described in Section 6.0 (p. 10-4).
sections.body: There are several other technologies related to, or an extension of, the four primary reinforcement applications of embankments over soft soils, MSE walls, reinforced soil slopes and soil nail walls (p. 10-4). These technologies are listed and described in Section 6.0: deep patching, shored MSE walls, stable feature MSE walls, shoot-in nails, screw-in nails and construction working platforms.
key_points: Related technologies are described in Section 6.0.
sections.applicability: Points to the related reinforced soil technologies covered at the end of Chapter 10.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.summary: Defines reinforced soil terms used in the manual: inclusion, reinforcement, reinforced soil, reinforced fill, retained backfill, MSE wall (face batter 20 degrees or less), RSS (face inclination less than 70 degrees), geosynthetics, facing, GRS and soil nails, plus acronyms (pp. 10-4 to 10-6).
sections.body: Terms are defined as follows (pp. 10-4 to 10-5). Inclusion: a generic term for all man-made elements incorporated in soil to improve its behavior (steel strips, geotextile sheets, steel or polymeric grids, steel nails, steel tendons between anchorage elements). Reinforcement: inclusions where soil-inclusion stress transfer occurs continuously along the inclusion. Reinforced soil: multiple layers of inclusions acting as reinforcement. Reinforced fill: the zone where reinforcements are placed in fill. Retained backfill: fill or in situ material behind the reinforced zone. MSE wall (MSEW): reinforced soil with planar reinforcement in fill structures with face inclinations of near vertical to slight batter (20 degrees or less). Reinforced soil slopes (RSS): planar reinforcement in earth-sloped structures with face inclinations of less than 70 degrees. Geosynthetics: flexible polymeric materials such as geotextiles, geogrids and geostraps. Facing: the component that prevents soil raveling between reinforcement rows (precast panels, dry cast modular blocks, gabions, WWM, shotcrete, timber lagging, cellular confinement, wrapped geosynthetics); it plays a minor structural role; for RSS usually WWM, geosynthetic wrap and/or erosion control material. GRS: geosynthetic reinforced soil with closely spaced reinforcement layers, designed by FHWA (2011a) on composite action rather than as inclusions. Soil nails: passive elements drilled and grouted sub-horizontally that work mainly in tension, transfer load by shear along the grout-ground interface and interact with the facing (after GEC 7). Acronyms: EOSS, HDPE, MSE, MSEW, PE, PET, PP, PVC, RSS (pp. 10-5 to 10-6).
key_points: MSE wall: face near vertical to slight batter, 20 degrees or less.
RSS: face inclination less than 70 degrees.
Reinforcement means continuous soil-inclusion stress transfer along the inclusion.
GRS is designed on composite action (FHWA 2011a), not as discrete inclusions.
Soil nails act mainly in tension, transferring load by grout-ground interface shear.
sections.applicability: Use for the meaning of reinforced soil terms and acronyms throughout Chapter 10.

sections.title: Reinforced Embankments
sections.summary: Section heading for reinforced embankments over soft soils: feasibility, applications, construction and materials, design overview, specifications and quality assurance, and cost data (pp. 10-7 to 10-18).
sections.body: Section 2.0 (p. 10-7) covers geosynthetic reinforced embankments over soft soils (EOSS): feasibility considerations (2.1), applications with advantages, feasibility evaluations, limitations and alternatives (2.2), construction and materials (2.3), design overview (2.4), construction specifications and quality assurance (2.5) and cost data (2.6).
sections.applicability: Entry point for reinforced embankments constructed over soft foundation soils.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Reinforced EOSS are cost-effective where foundation soils are too weak for the planned embankment; one or more high-strength geotextile or geogrid layers at the base reinforce it. Reinforcement can reduce foundation displacement but not total settlement or time to primary consolidation (p. 10-7).
sections.body: Reinforced EOSS structures are cost-effective alternatives for many applications where foundation soils are too weak to support the weight and geometry of the planned embankment (p. 10-7). One or more layers of high strength geotextile or geogrid are generally used at the embankment-to-foundation interface. Reinforced EOSS offer significant technical and cost advantages over the conventional excavate-and-replace technique. However, while a reinforced EOSS may reduce the displacement of foundation soil, it will not decrease the total anticipated embankment settlement or the time to achieve primary consolidation. Other techniques or combinations may be best where the rate and/or magnitude of settlement is of concern; for example, reinforced embankments have been combined with prefabricated vertical drains (Chapter 2) to increase the rate of settlement and with lightweight fills (Chapter 3) to decrease total settlement.
key_points: Basal reinforcement: one or more layers of high strength geotextile or geogrid.
Does not reduce total settlement or time to primary consolidation.
May be combined with PVDs (Chapter 2) or lightweight fill (Chapter 3).
sections.applicability: Applies when screening basal reinforcement for embankments on weak foundation soils.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Common application: embankment, dike or levee over very soft saturated silt, clay or peat, with reinforcement strong direction perpendicular to the centerline under plane strain; reinforcement provides stability until the foundation consolidates and gains strength. Geotextiles may also act as separators (pp. 10-7 to 10-8).
sections.body: The common application is an embankment, dike or levee constructed over very soft, saturated silt, clay or peat layers (Figure 10-1, p. 10-7). The reinforcement is usually placed with its strong direction perpendicular to the embankment centerline, and plane strain conditions are assumed. Generally the reinforcement provides stability until the underlying soft soils consolidate, gain strength and can support the embankment. Additional reinforcement with its strong direction parallel to the centerline may be required at the ends of the embankment (e.g., at a bridge abutment). Geotextiles may also be used as separators for displacement-type embankment construction (Holtz 1989) and as stabilization layers to support construction or ground modification equipment (Chapter 9) (p. 10-8). In that case the geotextile provides no significant reinforcement but acts primarily as a separator to keep the embankment intact as it displaces the subgrade; its design is based on constructability, survivability and filtration requirements, and a high elongation material may be selected.
key_points: Strong direction perpendicular to centerline; plane strain assumed.
Reinforcement needed only until the foundation gains strength by consolidation.
Longitudinal reinforcement may be needed at embankment ends (e.g., abutments).
Separator use: design on constructability, survivability and filtration.
figures: Figure 10-1: Common reinforced embankment application. (after Bonaparte and Christopher 1987; p. 10-7)
sections.applicability: Applies to embankments, dikes and levees over very soft saturated silt, clay or peat.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (10.2.2.1.1, printed 2.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (10.2.2.1.2, printed 2.1.2.2) of reinforced embankments.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of reinforced embankments, 10.2.2.1.1 (printed 2.1.2.1) and 10.2.2.1.2 (printed 2.1.2.2); it has no text of its own. (p. 10-8)
sections.applicability: Use when weighing a reinforced embankment against other soft-ground treatments.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Printed 2.1.2.1. Against excavate-and-replace and other technologies, geosynthetic reinforced EOSS raise the design global factor of safety and embankment height, reduce or eliminate side berms and foundation displacement (less fill), reduce differential settlement, and need no specialty contractor (p. 10-8).
sections.body: Printed with the number 2.1.2.1 under 2.2.1, a slip in the print's numbering. Geosynthetic reinforced EOSS have many advantages compared with the conventional excavate and replace technique and with other alternative technologies. Reinforced embankments provide an increase in the design global factor of safety and height of the embankment; reduction or elimination of stabilizing side berms, thus reducing fill requirements; reduction in displacement of foundation soil during construction, potentially reducing fill requirements; and reduction in differential settlement. Most general contractors can construct GREs, and specialty contractors are not required. (p. 10-8)
key_points: Increases design global factor of safety and achievable height.
Reduces or eliminates side berms and foundation displacement.
Reduces differential settlement; no specialty contractor needed.
sections.applicability: Use when weighing a reinforced embankment against other soft-ground treatments.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Printed 2.1.2.2. Total settlement will likely not be reduced, nor the time to primary consolidation; detailed field observations of pore pressures, total settlement and rate of settlement are generally required during construction (p. 10-8).
sections.body: Printed with the number 2.1.2.2 under 2.2.1, a slip in the print's numbering. Potential disadvantages that may be associated with a reinforced embankment project: the magnitude of total settlement will likely not be reduced; the time to achieve primary consolidation is not reduced; and detailed field observations are generally required during construction to monitor pore pressures, total settlement, and rate of settlement. (p. 10-8)
key_points: Does not reduce total settlement or consolidation time.
Requires monitoring of pore pressures and settlement during construction.
sections.applicability: Use when weighing a reinforced embankment against other soft-ground treatments.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Feasibility of a reinforced embankment: first consider a no-build or realignment alternative, a structure, or foundation soil modification; problem soils can be improved by reducing the load, replacing them, improving strength and compressibility, transferring loads or reinforcing (Broms 1979; Holtz 1989). The geotechnical, environmental and site subsections assume a reinforced embankment was selected (pp. 10-8 to 10-9).
sections.body: For problem foundations, three basic choices are evaluated first: a no-build or realignment alternative, placing the roadway on a structure, or some type of foundation soil modification (p. 10-8). Problem foundation soils can be improved by reducing the load, replacing poor soils, increasing shear strength and reducing compressibility, transferring loads to more competent soils, and reinforcing the embankment and/or its foundation (Broms 1979; Holtz 1989) (p. 10-9). Holtz (1989) discusses these alternatives and gives guidance on when embankment reinforcement is feasible; other ground modification options are presented in other chapters. The discussions that follow, 10.2.2.2.1 to 10.2.2.2.3 (printed 2.1.3.1 to 2.1.3.3), assume alternative foundation treatments have been considered and a reinforced embankment has been selected. (pp. 10-8 to 10-9)
key_points: First choices: no-build or realignment, a structure, or foundation soil modification.
Improvement routes: reduce load, replace soils, improve strength and compressibility, transfer loads, reinforce (Broms 1979; Holtz 1989).
sections.applicability: Applies to evaluating whether a reinforced embankment is feasible on a soft-ground site.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Printed 2.1.3.1. A reinforced embankment can be built over any depth of soft soil; check lateral squeeze where the soft layer is shallow relative to the embankment width. A comprehensive investigation with high quality undisturbed samples is key; settlement analyses cover primary, secondary, total and differential settlement in both directions (p. 10-9).
sections.body: Printed with the number 2.1.3.1 under 2.2.2, a slip in the print's numbering. A reinforced embankment can be constructed over any depth of soft soils, unlike other options that have depth limits. If the depth of soft soils is small relative to the width of the embankment, an additional stability mode of lateral squeeze failure should be examined. A comprehensive subsurface investigation program is a key element for successful design and construction; high quality, undisturbed soil samples are required for determination of engineering properties. Settlement analyses must assess primary, secondary, total and differential settlements, both transversely and longitudinally. (p. 10-9)
key_points: Reinforced embankments can be built over any depth of soft soil.
Check lateral squeeze where soft soil depth is small relative to embankment width.
Settlement analyses: primary, secondary, total and differential, both directions.
sections.applicability: Applies to evaluating whether a reinforced embankment is feasible on a soft-ground site.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Printed 2.1.3.2. Embankments on soft soils are often in wetlands, so the allowable width of wetland disturbance may govern; contaminated foundation soils or groundwater can stay in place, capped by the reinforced embankment (p. 10-9).
sections.body: Printed with the number 2.1.3.2 under 2.2.2, a slip in the print's numbering. Embankments on soft soils are often constructed in wetlands; the selection of an embankment construction option, and the design of a reinforced soil embankment option, may be impacted by the allowable width of wetland disturbance. Another consideration is whether the foundation soils and/or groundwater are contaminated and, if so, whether they can remain in place undisturbed or need to be treated if removed. A reinforced embankment leaves the underlying foundation soils in place and caps them with the embankment fill. (p. 10-9)
key_points: Wetland disturbance width can govern selection.
Contaminated foundation soils can stay in place, capped by the embankment fill.
sections.applicability: Applies to evaluating whether a reinforced embankment is feasible on a soft-ground site.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Printed 2.1.3.3. Existing vegetation, groundwater level and foundation strength dictate construction methods for the initial lifts; FHWA (2008a) covers site clearing, geosynthetic placement and fill placement and compaction (pp. 10-9 to 10-10).
sections.body: Printed with the number 2.1.3.3 under 2.2.2, a slip in the print's numbering. The existing vegetation, groundwater level, and strength of the underlying foundation soils will dictate construction methods for the initial lifts of the embankment. See FHWA (2008a) for site clearing, geosynthetic reinforcement placement, and embankment fill placement and compaction techniques for reinforced soil embankments. (pp. 10-9 to 10-10)
key_points: Vegetation, groundwater and foundation strength set the methods for the first lifts.
FHWA (2008a): site clearing, geosynthetic placement, fill placement and compaction.
sections.applicability: Applies to evaluating whether a reinforced embankment is feasible on a soft-ground site.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of reinforced embankments: total settlement is not significantly reduced; field instrumentation and monitoring are generally required to measure pore pressures and control fill placement rate; used alone it is not suited to projects that cannot wait for consolidation (p. 10-10).
sections.body: The total settlement magnitude will not be significantly reduced from the unreinforced embankment option (p. 10-10). Generally a field instrumentation and monitoring program is required to measure pore pressures in the foundation soils, maintain adequate safety factors and oversee the rate of embankment fill placement. When used alone, this technology is not appropriate for projects that cannot accommodate the time necessary for consolidation of the underlying foundation soils.
key_points: Total settlement not significantly reduced.
Instrumentation needed to control the rate of fill placement.
Alone, unsuitable where consolidation time cannot be accommodated.
sections.applicability: Use to judge whether schedule or settlement limits rule out a reinforced embankment alone.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions
sections.summary: Alternatives to reinforced EOSS: excavation and replacement for shallow soft soils, prefabricated vertical drains with preloading, deep dynamic compaction, vibro-compaction, lightweight fills and column supported embankments, chosen by soil type, depth and strength and project constraints (p. 10-10).
sections.body: Reinforcement is one of many technologies for EOSS (p. 10-10). If the soft soils extend only to a relatively shallow depth, excavation and replacement is a typical and cost-effective alternative. Other ground modification alternatives are prefabricated vertical drains and fill preloading (Chapter 2), deep dynamic compaction (Chapter 4), vibro-compaction (Chapter 4), lightweight fills (Chapter 3), and column supported embankments with or without a load transfer platform (Chapter 6). Applicability of reinforcement and of these alternatives depends on the type, depth and strength of the foundation soils, and project constraints and risks should be factored into the selection.
key_points: Shallow soft soil: excavation and replacement is typical and cost-effective.
Others: PVDs with preload, DDC, vibro-compaction, lightweight fill, column supported embankments.
sections.applicability: Applies to comparing ground modification options for embankments over soft soils.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: General construction requirements for geosynthetic reinforced embankments are in FHWA (2008a); the section gives the general construction sequence, and the primary materials are the geosynthetic reinforcement and the embankment fill soils (p. 10-10).
sections.body: General construction requirements and guidance for geosynthetic reinforced embankments are presented in FHWA (2008a) (p. 10-10). The section presents the general sequence of reinforced embankment construction (2.3.1). The primary materials used in construction are the geosynthetic soil reinforcement (2.3.2) and the embankment fill soils (2.3.3).
key_points: Construction guidance: FHWA (2008a).
Primary materials: geosynthetic reinforcement and embankment fill.
sections.applicability: Entry point for construction and materials of reinforced embankments over soft soils.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of reinforced embankments on soft foundations: improper fill placement can damage the geosynthetic, cause nonuniform settlement or failure. Steps: prepare subgrade leaving stumps and root mat, place geosynthetic, place and compact fill, monitor with piezometers and settlement plates (pp. 10-10 to 10-11).
sections.body: Construction procedures for reinforced embankments on soft foundations are extremely important; improper fill placement can lead to geosynthetic damage, nonuniform settlements and even embankment failure (pp. 10-10 to 10-11). With low ground pressure equipment, a properly selected geosynthetic and proper fill placement procedures, these problems can essentially be eliminated. The primary steps (details in FHWA 2008a) are: (1) prepare the subgrade, leaving tree stumps, grass and root mass in place to support construction equipment; (2) geosynthetic placement, including orientation, roll width and length, sewing, manual tension, and inspection and repair; (3) fill placement, spreading and compaction, including placement sequence, initial lift height and compaction and subsequent lifts, with procedures differing between extremely soft and moderate foundations; and (4) construction monitoring with piezometers, settlement plates and fill thickness measurements.
key_points: Use low ground pressure equipment.
Leave stumps, grass and root mass in place for equipment support.
Fill placement sequence differs for extremely soft versus moderate foundations.
Monitor with piezometers, settlement plates and fill thickness measurements.
sections.applicability: Applies to the field sequence for building geosynthetic reinforced embankments on soft ground.

sections.title: Geosynthetic Reinforcement
sections.summary: Geosynthetic strength requirements, including seam strength, come from analysis and design; specifications must also consider drainage, construction conditions and environment. Table 10-1 lists mechanical, hydraulic, constructability and longevity properties required for reinforced embankments (pp. 10-11 to 10-12).
sections.body: Geosynthetic strength requirements, including seam strength, are quantified in the analysis and design process (p. 10-11). Besides tensile and frictional properties, the specification must consider drainage requirements, construction conditions and environmental factors. Table 10-1 (p. 10-12) lists the required properties. Design requirements, mechanical: tensile strength, tensile modulus and seam strength (all by wide width strength), tension creep (tension creep), and soil-geosynthetic friction (soil-geosynthetic friction angle). Design requirements, hydraulic: piping resistance (apparent opening size) and permeability (permeability). Constructability requirements: tensile strength (grab strength), puncture resistance (puncture resistance) and tear resistance (trapezoidal tear). Longevity: UV stability if exposed (UV resistance) and soil compatibility where required (chemical; biological). See FHWA (2008a) for discussion of these properties and for construction survivability requirements.
key_points: Tensile strength, modulus and seam strength are specified by wide width strength.
Hydraulic: apparent opening size and permeability.
Constructability: grab strength, puncture resistance, trapezoidal tear.
Longevity: UV resistance if exposed; chemical and biological compatibility where required.

sections.applicability: Use when specifying geosynthetic reinforcement properties for embankments over soft soils.

sections.title: Embankment Fill
sections.summary: The first lift above the geosynthetic should be free-draining granular fill for drainage of excess pore water and good frictional interaction; lower permeability fill may be used above if strain compatibility is checked, with horizontal geocomposite strip drains considered (pp. 10-12 to 10-13).
sections.body: The first lift of fill just above the geosynthetic reinforcement should be a free-draining granular material (p. 10-12). It serves as a drainage layer for excess pore water dissipating from the underlying soils and provides good frictional interaction between the geosynthetic and the embankment fill. Other lower permeability (preferably granular) fill may be used above this layer provided the strain compatibility of the geosynthetic is evaluated with respect to the fill. If lower permeability fill is used, horizontal prefabricated geocomposite drains (e.g., strip drains) placed directly on the foundation soil should also be considered to provide drainage and facilitate consolidation (p. 10-13).
key_points: First lift above geosynthetic: free-draining granular material.
Lower permeability fill above requires a strain compatibility check.
Consider horizontal geocomposite strip drains on the foundation soil.
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting fill for geosynthetic reinforced embankments over soft soils.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Reinforced embankments are designed against failure; Figure 10-2 shows the three failure modes that set the required stability analyses. Settlement and reinforcement creep are also considered; the end of construction is most critical, so reinforcement need only function until the foundation gains strength (p. 10-13).
sections.body: As with ordinary embankments on soft soils, the basic design approach is to design against failure (p. 10-13). The potential failure modes are illustrated in Figure 10-2; the three possible modes indicate the types of stability analyses required. Settlement of the embankment and potential creep of the reinforcement must also be considered, although creep is only a factor if the creep rate in the reinforcement is faster than the rate of strength gain in the foundation soils due to consolidation. Because the most critical condition for embankment stability is at the end of construction, the reinforcement only has to function until the foundation soils gain sufficient strength to support the embankment (FHWA 2008a).
key_points: Three failure modes define the required stability analyses.
Creep matters only if it outpaces foundation strength gain.
End of construction is the critical condition.
figures: Figure 10-2: Reinforced embankment failure modes. (FHWA 2008a, after Haliburton et al. 1978; p. 10-13)
sections.applicability: Applies to the design approach for basal-reinforced embankments on soft foundations.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Stability and settlement calculations use conventional procedures modified for the reinforcement. Total stress analysis is usual and conservative (no strength gain); effective stress analysis needs reliable pore pressure estimates and Ko-consolidated undrained triaxial tests, plus field piezometers to control fill rate (p. 10-14).
sections.body: Stability and settlement calculations use conventional geotechnical design procedures modified only for the presence of the reinforcement (p. 10-14). Stability of an embankment over soft soil is usually determined by the total stress method, which is conservative because it generally assumes no strength gain in the compressible soil; FHWA (2008a) uses the total stress approach because it is simple and appropriate for reinforcement design (Holtz 1989). Stability can always be calculated in effective stresses with effective stress strength parameters, but that requires an accurate estimate of field pore pressures during design, high quality undisturbed samples and Ko consolidated-undrained triaxial tests. Because in situ pore pressures are hard to predict before construction, field pore pressure measurements with high quality piezometers are essential during construction to control the rate of filling. Accounting for strength gain with controlled rate (staged) construction allows lower strength and lower cost reinforcement, but construction time may increase significantly and the costs of investigation, testing, analyses, instrumentation and inspection are greater (FHWA 2008a).
key_points: Total stress analysis: usual, simple and conservative.
Effective stress analysis needs pore pressure estimates and Ko-CU triaxial tests.
Piezometers are essential to control filling rate.
Staged construction allows lower strength reinforcement at the cost of time and testing.
sections.applicability: Use when choosing total or effective stress analysis for reinforced embankment stability.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Table 10-2 lists the 15-step total stress design procedure for reinforced embankments: dimensions and loads, soil profile and properties, fill properties, factors of safety, bearing, rotational and lateral spreading stability, required modulus J, longitudinal strength, other properties, settlement, construction and monitoring (pp. 10-14 to 10-15).
sections.body: A step-by-step total stress design procedure is listed in Table 10-2 (p. 10-15); substeps and commentary are in FHWA (2008a). Step 1: define embankment dimensions and loading conditions. Step 2: establish the soil profile and engineering properties of the foundation soil. Step 3: obtain engineering properties of embankment fill. Step 4: establish minimum appropriate factors of safety and operational settlement criteria. Step 5: check bearing capacity. Step 6: check rotational shear stability. Step 7: check lateral spreading (sliding) stability. Step 8: establish tolerable geosynthetic deformation requirements and calculate the required reinforcement modulus, J, based on wide width (ASTM D4595) tensile testing. Step 9: establish geosynthetic tensile strength requirements in the longitudinal direction (along the embankment alignment). Step 10: establish geosynthetic modulus, seam strength, soil-geosynthetic friction, and survivability and construction properties. Step 11: estimate magnitude and rate of settlement. Step 12: establish construction sequence and procedures. Step 13: establish construction observation and monitoring requirements. Step 14: hold preconstruction meetings. Step 15: observe construction and build with confidence.
key_points: Total stress procedure in 15 steps (Table 10-2).
Stability checks: bearing capacity, rotational shear, lateral spreading (sliding).
Required reinforcement modulus J from tolerable deformation, based on wide width tests (ASTM D4595).
Separate longitudinal tensile strength requirement.
sections.applicability: Applies to the design sequence for geosynthetic reinforced embankments using total stress analysis.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary reference for total stress design of reinforced embankments is FHWA (2008a); additional references include FHWA (1985), Bonaparte and Christopher (1987), the Canadian Foundation Engineering Manual (2006), Li and Rowe (2001) for PVDs with reinforcement and Rowe and Soderman (1985, 1986) for peats (p. 10-15).
sections.body: The primary reference for total stress design of reinforced embankments is FHWA (2008a), Geosynthetic Design and Construction Guidelines (Holtz, Christopher and Berg; FHWA-HI-07-092) (p. 10-15). Additional references include FHWA (1985), Bonaparte and Christopher (1987) and the Canadian Foundation Engineering Manual (2006). See Li and Rowe (2001) for an analysis method combining prefabricated vertical drains (Chapter 2) with geosynthetic reinforcement. For reinforced embankments over fibrous peats, see Rowe and Soderman (1985) for peat underlain by a firm base and Rowe and Soderman (1986) for peat underlain by a soft cohesive layer.
key_points: Primary: FHWA (2008a).
PVDs with reinforcement: Li and Rowe (2001).
Fibrous peats: Rowe and Soderman (1985, 1986).
sections.applicability: Use to find detailed design methods for reinforced embankments, including over peat or with PVDs.

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Heading for reinforced embankment construction specifications and quality assurance: specification development, a summary of quality assurance with Table 10-3, and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (pp. 10-16 to 10-18).
sections.body: Section 2.5 (p. 10-16) gives an overview of construction specifications and quality assurance for reinforced embankments: specification development (2.5.1), a summary of quality assurance with Table 10-3 (2.5.2), and a summary of instrumentation monitoring and construction control (2.5.3).
sections.applicability: Entry point for specifying and controlling construction of reinforced embankments.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Reinforcement requirements for soft-ground embankments are project and site specific, so standard specifications with suggested properties are not appropriate; special provisions or a project specification are needed. FHWA (2008a) presents an example method-type state DOT specification (p. 10-16).
sections.body: Because the reinforcement requirements for soft-ground embankment construction are project and site specific, standard specifications that include suggested geosynthetic properties are not appropriate, and special provisions or a separate project specification must be used (p. 10-16). An example reinforced embankment specification that includes most items to be considered on a project is presented in FHWA (2008a); it is a state department of transportation method-type specification.
key_points: Use special provisions or a project specification, not a standard specification.
Example method-type specification in FHWA (2008a).
sections.applicability: Applies to writing specifications for geosynthetic reinforced embankments on soft ground.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Contractor procedures are crucial for reinforced embankments on very soft foundations, so competent inspection is essential to verify the specified material, prevent damage and enforce the construction sequence. Table 10-3 lists typical QA components (pp. 10-16 to 10-17).
sections.body: The construction procedures used by a contractor are crucial to the success of a reinforced embankment on a very soft foundation, so competent and professional construction inspection is absolutely essential (p. 10-16). Field personnel must be trained to observe every phase and ensure that (1) the specified reinforcement is delivered, (2) the geosynthetic is not damaged during construction, and (3) the specified sequence of construction operations is explicitly followed. Table 10-3 (p. 10-17, after GeoTechTools) lists typical, not exhaustive, QA components: material-related procedures (embankment soil shear strength, reinforcement tensile seam strength); process control procedures (monitor foundation pore water pressure, settlement and fill thickness, reinforcement placement geometries); material measurement values (soil shear strength tests, reinforcement and seam coupon tests, manufacturer's certification); process control measurement values (pore pressure, lift thickness, settlement, placement geometry, reinforcement quantities); material performance criteria (reinforcement strain, foundation strength gain over time); system behavior criteria (settlement, pore pressure, lateral deformation of embankment and foundation); and emerging methods (intelligent geosynthetic, automated instrumentation).
key_points: Inspection must confirm specified material, no damage, and specified construction sequence.
QA includes pore pressure, settlement, fill thickness and placement geometry monitoring.
Emerging QA: intelligent geosynthetics and automated instrumentation.
tables: Table 10-3: Typical Components of Reinforced Embankment Quality Assurance (p. 10-17)
sections.applicability: Use when planning inspection and QA for reinforced embankments on soft foundations.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Instrumentation for reinforced embankments should at minimum include piezometers, settlement points and surface survey monuments, with optional inclinometers, to verify design assumptions and control and usually expedite construction. Every instrument must answer a specific question (pp. 10-17 to 10-18).
sections.body: As noted in Table 10-2, construction observation is a design step; it includes the construction QA program, instrumentation installation and monitoring (p. 10-17). As a minimum, instrumentation should include piezometers, settlement points and surface survey monuments; inclinometers may be installed to observe lateral movement with depth. The purpose of instrumentation on soft ground reinforcement projects is not research but to verify design assumptions and to control and, usually, expedite the construction schedule (e.g., by a more accurate determination of the time required for settlement) (p. 10-18). The first step in planning a monitoring program is to define the purpose of the measurements: every instrument should be selected and placed to help answer a specific question; if there is no question, there should be no instrumentation. The most significant parameters should be selected, with care to identify secondary parameters that may influence primary ones.
key_points: Minimum: piezometers, settlement points, surface survey monuments; inclinometers optional.
Purpose: verify design assumptions and control or expedite construction.
If there is no question, there should be no instrumentation.
sections.applicability: Applies to instrumentation planning for staged or reinforced embankments over soft soils.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Cost analysis for a geosynthetic reinforced embankment (FHWA 2008a) includes geosynthetic cost, site preparation, geosynthetic placement with or without a working table, and fill material including allowance for subsidence, using free-draining granular fill next to the geosynthetic (p. 10-18).
sections.body: The cost analysis for a geosynthetic reinforced embankment (FHWA 2008a) includes (p. 10-18): (1) geosynthetic cost, including purchase price, factory prefabrication and shipping; (2) site preparation, including clearing and grubbing and working table preparation; (3) geosynthetic placement, related to field workability, with no working table or with a working table; and (4) fill material, including purchasing, hauling, dumping, compaction and an allowance for additional fill due to embankment subsidence. Free-draining granular fill should be used for the lifts adjacent to the geosynthetic to provide good reinforcement interaction and drainage.
key_points: Cost items: geosynthetic, site preparation, placement, fill (with subsidence allowance).
sections.applicability: Use to assemble the cost elements of a geosynthetic reinforced embankment.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Typical pay items for geosynthetic reinforced embankments: geosynthetic by the square yard in place, granular material by the ton and embankment material by the cubic yard; operations are common except low ground pressure equipment, and mobilization costs are generally negligible (p. 10-18).
sections.body: Typical contract pay items and units for geosynthetic reinforced embankments are (p. 10-18): geosynthetic (fabric or grid) measured by the square yard in place; granular material measured by the ton; and embankment material measured by the cubic yard. Geosynthetic reinforced embankments are built with operations common to highway construction projects, except that low ground pressure equipment (e.g., wide track dozers) is not always common. Generally, mobilization costs are negligible.
key_points: Geosynthetic: square yard in place; granular material: ton; embankment: cubic yard.
Mobilization costs generally negligible.
sections.applicability: Applies to pay items and cost estimating for reinforced embankments.

sections.title: Reinforced Soil Walls
sections.summary: Section heading for reinforced soil (MSE) walls: feasibility considerations, design overview, construction and materials, construction specifications and quality assurance, and cost data (pp. 10-19 to 10-42).
sections.body: Section 3.0 (p. 10-19) covers mechanically stabilized earth (MSE) walls and GRS walls: feasibility considerations (3.1), design overview (3.2), construction and materials (3.3), specifications and quality assurance (3.4) and cost data (3.5).
sections.applicability: Entry point for MSE and geosynthetic reinforced soil walls in transportation works.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: MSE walls are cost-effective alternatives where reinforced concrete or gravity walls have been used, with significant technical and cost advantages on poor foundations; eliminating piles and pile caps has given savings greater than 50 percent on completed projects (p. 10-19).
sections.body: MSE wall (MSEW) structures are cost-effective alternatives for most applications where reinforced concrete or gravity type walls have traditionally been used to retain soil (p. 10-19). They also offer significant technical and cost advantages over conventional reinforced concrete retaining structures, especially at sites with poor foundation conditions. In such cases, eliminating the cost of foundation improvements such as piles and pile caps that conventional structures may need has resulted in cost savings of greater than 50 percent on completed projects.
key_points: Savings greater than 50 percent where piles and pile caps are avoided.
sections.applicability: Applies to screening MSE walls against conventional concrete retaining walls.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: MSE wall applications: bridge abutments and wing walls, restricted right-of-way, steep terrain, unstable ground and poor foundations, elevated urban interstates, very tall walls (138 ft exposed height), and temporary walls for detours, temporary abutments and phased construction (pp. 10-19 to 10-22).
sections.body: Representative uses of MSE walls are shown in Figure 10-3 (p. 10-19): bridge abutments and wing walls, and areas where right-of-way is restricted so that an embankment or excavation with stable side slopes cannot be built. They are particularly suited to economical construction in steep-sided terrain, in ground subject to slope instability, or where foundation soils are poor. A typical application of an elevated interstate in an urban area is shown in Figure 10-4. The tallest MSE wall in the United States to date has an exposed height of 138 feet at its tallest section, built for an airport third-runway project (Figure 10-5). Temporary MSE walls have been especially cost-effective for temporary detours during highway reconstruction, supporting temporary roadway embankments and temporary bridge abutments (Figure 10-6) (p. 10-21). MSE walls are also used as temporary support of permanent roadway embankments for phased construction (Figure 10-7) (p. 10-22).
key_points: Uses: abutments, wing walls, restricted ROW, steep terrain, unstable ground, poor foundations.
Tallest U.S. MSE wall: 138 ft exposed height.
Temporary MSE walls are cost-effective for detours and phased construction.
figures: Figure 10-3: Representative MSE wall application: retaining wall (top left), access ramp (top right), waterfront structure (bottom left) and bridge abutment (bottom right). (GEC 11; p. 10-20)
Figure 10-4: MSE wall construction on an urban elevated interstate project (project name omitted). (GEC 11; p. 10-20)
Figure 10-5: Airport runway extension MSE wall (airport name omitted). (GEC 11; p. 10-21)
Figure 10-6: MSE walls to support temporary bridge abutment and roadway embankment. (GEC 11; p. 10-21)
Figure 10-7: MSE wall used to temporarily support a permanent roadway embankment for phased construction. (GEC 11; p. 10-22)
sections.applicability: Use to identify suitable permanent and temporary applications of MSE walls.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (10.3.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (10.3.1.2.2) of MSE walls.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of MSE walls, 10.3.1.2.1 and 10.3.1.2.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 10-22)
sections.applicability: Use when weighing MSE walls against conventional concrete retaining walls.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: MSE walls build faster with smaller equipment and no curing, need no special skills, less site preparation, front space and right-of-way, tolerate deformation without rigid foundations, are cost effective and feasible above 100 ft; likely cheaper than other walls above about 10 ft; better seismic performance than rigid walls.
sections.body: Compared with reinforced concrete and gravity walls, MSE walls: are significantly faster to build with simple procedures, smaller equipment and no concrete curing; need no special skills; need less site preparation and less space in front; reduce right-of-way; need no rigid, unyielding foundation, since they tolerate deformation; are cost effective; and are technically feasible above 100 feet. Pre-manufactured materials, rapid construction and competition among proprietary systems have cut cost (p. 10-23); MSE walls are likely more economical than other systems for walls higher than about 10 feet or where a conventional wall would need special foundations. Their flexibility under poor foundations is among their greatest advantages, and in seismic zones they have shown higher resistance than rigid concrete walls. (pp. 10-22 to 10-23)
key_points: Faster construction, no curing, smaller equipment (p. 10-22).
Feasible above 100 ft; likely cheaper above about 10 ft (p. 10-23).
Tolerate deformation; better seismic performance than rigid walls (p. 10-23).
sections.applicability: Use when weighing MSE walls against conventional concrete retaining walls.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: MSE walls need a relatively large space behind the face for reinforcement, select granular fill, often shared design responsibility between suppliers and owners, and leave no-dig zones in the reinforced section.
sections.body: General potential disadvantages: a relatively large space (e.g., excavation in a cut) is needed behind the face for reinforcement; select granular fill is required; design responsibility is often shared between material suppliers and owners; and the reinforced section is a no dig zone (e.g., for utility installation or repair). (p. 10-23)
key_points: Large space behind the face; select granular fill (p. 10-23).
No dig zones within the reinforced section (p. 10-23).
sections.applicability: Use when weighing MSE walls against conventional concrete retaining walls.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental, site and aesthetic feasibility of MSE walls (10.3.1.3.1 to 10.3.1.3.4).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of MSE walls, 10.3.1.3.1 to 10.3.1.3.4; it has no text of its own. (p. 10-23)
sections.applicability: Applies to geotechnical, environmental, site and aesthetic screening of MSE wall sites.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Inadequate exploration missing soft soils causes most distress, rarely collapse. Establish bearing, global stability, settlement and groundwater; as a first approximation available shear strength must be at least 2.0 to 2.5 times the fill weight, else consider ground improvement; then check differential settlement for facing and phasing.
sections.body: An adequate subsurface investigation is key; distress is often traced to exploration that missed soft soils, causing local differential settlement and facing distress, and in a few extreme cases complete foundation failure and collapse. Foundation properties should establish bearing resistance, global stability, settlement potential and groundwater. As a first-order check, the foundation must carry the fill: over soft compressible soils, preliminary stability analyses must show enough shear strength, and as a rough first approximation the available shear strength must be at least 2.0 to 2.5 times the weight of the fill structure (p. 10-24); otherwise ground improvement must be considered. Where strength is marginal to adequate, preliminary settlement analyses along and across the wall, a second-order check, guide facing type and construction phasing. (pp. 10-23 to 10-24)
key_points: Inadequate exploration of soft soils is a common cause of distress (p. 10-23).
Available shear strength at least 2.0 to 2.5 times the fill weight (p. 10-23).
Differential settlement guides facing type and phasing (p. 10-24).
sections.applicability: Applies to geotechnical, environmental, site and aesthetic screening of MSE wall sites.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Ground aggressiveness governs reinforcement choice: for steel, chlorides and sulfates above about 200 ppm or pH < 5 accelerate corrosion and pH > 10 strips galvanizing; PET degrades in highly alkaline or acidic ground, polyolefins only in some acidic metal-bearing ground. Dry-cast MBW units suffer freeze-thaw with deicing salts.
sections.body: The aggressiveness of the in-situ ground governs reinforcement type and performance, including later deicing salts or fertilizers. For steel, chloride and sulfate salts generally above 200 ppm accelerate corrosion, as does pH less than 5 (FHWA 2009); pH > 10 accelerates loss of galvanization. Polyester (PET) degrades in highly alkaline or acidic ground; polyolefins appear to degrade only in certain highly acidic, metal-bearing conditions (e.g., mine waste) (FHWA 2009). For facings, deicing salt spray governs: dry-cast concrete MBW units are susceptible to freeze-thaw degradation with deicing salts in cold climates, though some vendors' mixes and processes give very durable units (see GEC 11). (p. 10-24)
key_points: Steel: chlorides/sulfates above about 200 ppm or pH < 5 accelerate corrosion (p. 10-24).
pH > 10 accelerates loss of galvanization; PET degrades at high or low pH (p. 10-24).
Dry-cast MBW units susceptible to freeze-thaw with deicing salts (p. 10-24).
sections.applicability: Applies to geotechnical, environmental, site and aesthetic screening of MSE wall sites.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: MSE walls suit fill-type walls and side-hill fills, where excavation is small; large cuts reduce but often do not remove the economy. Poor or remote access favors lightweight facings (wrapped geosynthetics, vegetation, metal skins, wire mesh, gabions, MBW units).
sections.body: MSE walls are particularly well suited to 'fill-type' walls and side-hill fills, where excavation may be small and the economy is kept; large cut volumes diminish it but often leave it viable (p. 10-25). Site access may dictate facing type and size: poor access or remote sites suit lightweight facings (geotextile or geogrid wrapped faces and vegetation, metal skins, welded wire mesh, gabions or MBW units) erected without heavy lifting equipment. (pp. 10-24 to 10-25)
key_points: Suited to fill-type walls and side-hill fills (p. 10-24).
Remote sites favor lightweight facings (p. 10-25).
sections.applicability: Applies to geotechnical, environmental, site and aesthetic screening of MSE wall sites.

sections.title: Aesthetics
sections.summary: Precast panels can take any texture and color for a premium seldom over 15% of facing cost (about 4 to 6% of total in-place cost); MBW facings cost about the same as panels except on small projects (under 4,000 ft2), where they save, and come in colors and finishes (GEC 11).
sections.body: Precast concrete facing panels may be cast in an unlimited variety of texture and color for a premium that seldom exceeds 15 percent of facing cost, on average a 4 to 6 percent increase in total in-place cost. Modular block wall facings are often comparable in cost to precast panels except on small projects (less than 4,000 square feet), where they save on erection equipment and on special made-to-order panels for irregular geometry; MBW facings come in color and many surface finishes (GEC 11). (p. 10-25)
key_points: Texture and color premium seldom over 15% of facing cost (p. 10-25).
MBW cheaper on projects under 4,000 ft2 (p. 10-25).
sections.applicability: Applies to geotechnical, environmental, site and aesthetic screening of MSE wall sites.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Per AASHTO LRFD (2014), MSE walls should not be used where non-drainage utilities are in the reinforced zone without access, where floodplain erosion or scour may undermine the fill, facing or footing, or where reinforcement is exposed to acid mine drainage or other aggressive water without specific studies (p. 10-25).
sections.body: The AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (2014) state that MSE walls should not be used under the following conditions (p. 10-25): when utilities other than highway drainage are to be constructed within the reinforced zone, unless access is provided to the utilities without disrupting reinforcements and breakage or rupture of utility lines will not have a detrimental effect on stability; where floodplain erosion or scour may undermine the reinforced fill zone, facing or any supporting footing; and with reinforcements exposed to surface or ground water contaminated by acid mine drainage, other industrial pollutants or other environmental conditions defined as aggressive in Article 7.3.6.3 of the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Construction Specifications (2010), unless environment-specific long-term corrosion or degradation studies are conducted.
key_points: No non-drainage utilities in the reinforced zone unless accessible without disrupting reinforcement.
Not where scour or floodplain erosion may undermine the wall.
Not in aggressive environments (AASHTO Construction Spec Art. 7.3.6.3) without specific studies.
sections.applicability: Use to check AASHTO conditions under which MSE walls should not be used.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions
sections.summary: Alternatives to MSE walls: cantilever, gravity, semi-gravity or counterfort concrete walls, or soil or reinforced slopes; in cuts, tieback, soil nail or nongravity cantilever walls, or a shored MSE combination; for waterfront walls, sheetpile walls are often more economical (p. 10-26).
sections.body: Cantilever, gravity, semi gravity or counterfort concrete walls, or soil embankments, are the usual alternatives to MSE walls and abutments; embankments may be conventional or reinforced soil slopes (Section 4.0) (p. 10-26). In cut situations, in situ walls such as tieback anchored walls, soil nailed walls or nongravity cantilevered walls are often more economical, although where right-of-way is limited a temporary or permanent in situ wall at the back of the reinforcement combined with a permanent MSE wall is often competitive; a permanent in situ wall at the back allows much shorter reinforcement (Section 6.2 and GEC 11). For waterfront or marine walls, sheetpile walls with or without anchorages that can be built in the wet are often, if not always, both more economical and more practical.
key_points: Fill situations: concrete walls or (reinforced) slopes.
Cut situations: anchored, soil nail or nongravity cantilever walls, or shored MSE.
Waterfront: sheetpile walls usually more economical and practical.
sections.applicability: Applies to comparing MSE walls with other wall types in fill, cut and waterfront settings.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: MSE walls are designed as a soil mass with discrete tension inclusions by the Simplified Method (ASD updated to LRFD), for near-vertical walls with uniform reinforcement and select fill; steel walls may use the Coherent Gravity Method; GRS walls are designed as a composite mass (FHWA 2011a), including GRS-IBS abutments (pp. 10-26 to 10-27).
sections.body: MSE walls are generally designed as a soil mass with discrete soil reinforcement modeled as tension inclusions (p. 10-26). The principal methodology is the Simplified Method, first established as an allowable strength design (ASD) method and updated to load and resistance factor design in the primary references. It is widely used for transportation walls that are near vertical, have uniform reinforcement lengths and use select granular reinforced fill; internal stability is independent of the facing. AASHTO (2014) and GEC 11 (2009) give guidance for deep facing elements in external stability, significantly battered walls and non-uniform reinforcement lengths. The Simplified Method applies to steel strip, steel mat, geogrid and geotextile reinforcements; per AASHTO (2014), internal loads for steel reinforced walls may be computed with the Coherent Gravity Method instead. Neither AASHTO (2014) nor GEC 11 gives design guidance for geosynthetic strap reinforcements. Alternatively, the reinforced soil may be designed as a composite mass: FHWA (2011a) gives an approach for closely spaced geosynthetic reinforced soil walls based on composite action, used in recent years for bridge abutments integrated into single span bridges (pp. 10-26 to 10-27). Closely spaced reinforcement with open-graded aggregate fill and a reinforced soil foundation supporting a bridge is a geosynthetic reinforced soil - integrated bridge system (GRS-IBS) (Figure 10-8), common for single span bridges over creeks and streams.
key_points: Simplified Method: reinforcement as tension inclusions; LRFD per AASHTO (2014) and GEC 11.
Coherent Gravity Method permitted for steel reinforced walls.
No AASHTO or GEC 11 design guidance for geosynthetic straps.
GRS and GRS-IBS designed on composite action (FHWA 2011a).

sections.applicability: Applies to choosing the design method for MSE and GRS walls and abutments.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: MSE wall design often involves shared responsibility: the wall system supplier designs internal and external stability with specifier-supplied or assumed soil properties, so the agency must clearly define design and material responsibilities and any agency-specific requirements (pp. 10-27 to 10-28).
sections.body: As previously noted, design of MSE wall systems often entails a shared design responsibility between material suppliers and the agency specifier/owner (pp. 10-27 to 10-28). The wall system supplier, often nationally rather than locally based, generally designs the wall for internal and external stability with soil properties supplied by the specifier or assumed. It is therefore imperative that the specifying agency clearly define design and material responsibilities, and any agency-specific design or detailing requirements that differ from the primary design references (Section 3.2.3).
key_points: Supplier typically designs internal and external stability.
Agency must define design and material responsibilities and agency-specific requirements.
sections.applicability: Use when setting responsibilities between agency and MSE wall supplier.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Table 10-4 lists the basic LRFD design steps for MSE walls with simple geometry: requirements, parameters, embedment and reinforcement length, loads, load and resistance factors, external stability (sliding, eccentricity, bearing, settlement), internal stability sub-steps, facing, global and compound stability and drainage (pp. 10-28 to 10-29).
sections.body: The basic design steps are listed in Table 10-4 (pp. 10-28 to 10-29, source GEC 11), for walls with simple geometries; steps vary with reinforcement type and additional steps are needed for complex cases such as true bridge abutments. Step 1: establish project requirements (geometry, permanent, transient and seismic loads, performance criteria, construction constraints). Step 2: establish project parameters (topography, subsurface conditions, reinforced fill and retained backfill properties). Step 3: estimate embedment depth, design height(s) and reinforcement length. Step 4: define nominal loads. Step 5: summarize load combinations, load factors and resistance factors. Step 6: evaluate external stability: sliding, eccentricity, bearing on foundation soil, settlement (service limit). Step 7: evaluate internal stability: select reinforcement type; define the critical failure surface; define unfactored loads; establish vertical layout; calculate factored horizontal stress and maximum tension at each level; calculate nominal and factored long-term tensile resistance; select grade and/or number of elements; calculate nominal and factored pullout resistance; check facing connection resistance; estimate lateral wall movements (service); check vertical movement and compression pads. Step 8: design facing elements. Step 9: assess overall global stability. Step 10: assess compound stability. Step 11: design subsurface and surface drainage. Detailed guidance and examples are in GEC 11.
key_points: External stability: sliding, eccentricity, bearing, settlement.
Internal stability: critical surface, maximum tension, long-term tensile resistance, pullout, connection.
Also facing design, global and compound stability, drainage.
The long-term tensile resistance step is listed but no equation for it is printed in this chapter; see GEC 11.
