sections.applicability: Applies to the LRFD design sequence for MSE walls of simple geometry.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary references for MSE wall design are AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (2014) and GEC 11 (2009); GRS-IBS walls may use FHWA (2011a, 2011b); NCMA (2009) is typically used for non-transportation MBW walls and some DOTs allow it for landscape walls only (pp. 10-29 to 10-30).
sections.body: There are two primary references for reinforced soil walls in transportation works (p. 10-29): AASHTO (2014) LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, 7th Edition with 2015 Interim Revisions, and GEC 11 (2009), Design and Construction of Mechanically Stabilized Earth Walls and Reinforced Soil Slopes (FHWA NHI-10-024 and NHI-10-025). Closely spaced geosynthetic reinforcements for bridges on a GRS-IBS can be designed with those references or with FHWA (2011a) Geosynthetic Reinforced Soil Integrated Bridge System, Interim Implementation Guide (FHWA-HRT-11-026) and FHWA (2011b) Synthesis Report (FHWA-HRT-11-027) (p. 10-30). MBW faced geosynthetic walls in transportation works are normally designed with either set; for non-transportation works they are typically designed with NCMA (2009) Design Manual for Segmental Retaining Walls. Some DOTs allow the NCMA method for landscape walls, but most do not allow it for structural wall applications.
key_points: Primary: AASHTO (2014) and GEC 11 (2009).
GRS-IBS: FHWA (2011a, 2011b).
NCMA (2009) mostly for non-transportation walls; most DOTs disallow it for structural walls.
sections.applicability: Use to find the governing design documents for MSE, GRS-IBS and MBW walls.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: General construction requirements for MSE walls are in AASHTO (2010) and GEC 11; walls are usually specified as a system from an approved products list, and a system- and agency-specific erection manual should be required from each vendor (p. 10-30).
sections.body: General construction requirements and guidance for MSE walls are presented in AASHTO (2010) and FHWA (GEC 11) (p. 10-30). As discussed in Section 3.4, MSE walls are most often specified as a system with an approved products (wall system) list established by the specifying DOT. A system-specific and agency-specific construction erection manual should be required from each vendor applying for pre-approval, and used by the contractor, inspectors and agency for construction. A variety of reinforcement and facing materials are used; they are summarized in this section, with detail in GEC 11, AASHTO (2010) and AASHTO (2014).
key_points: Usually specified as a system from an approved products list.
Require a system- and agency-specific erection manual from each vendor.
sections.applicability: Entry point for MSE wall construction sequence and materials.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: MSE wall construction steps: prepare and test subgrade, improve unstable foundations, place an unreinforced 6-inch concrete leveling pad, erect and brace the first facing row, place and compact fill (95-100% of T 99, loose lifts not over 12 in., typically 8-in. compacted), place and connect reinforcement, repeat, then barriers and copings (pp. 10-30 to 10-32).
sections.body: General steps (pp. 10-30 to 10-32): Preparation of subgrade: remove unsuitable materials, strip organic matter, vegetation and slide debris, compact the subgrade, and confirm suitability by observation and tests (e.g., proof rolling, dynamic cone penetrometer). In unstable foundation areas, use ground improvement (excavation and replacement, dynamic compaction, stone columns) before erection. Leveling pad: generally an unreinforced 6-inch thick concrete pad, often 6 inches or more wider than the facing element, wider under curves; it guides panel erection and is not a structural foundation; it is not used with welded wire or geosynthetic wrapped facings. First row of facing: with precast panels, alternating full and half-height panels, externally braced; later rows are wedged and clamped; full blocks without shoring are used with MBW or large wet cast units. Reinforced fill is placed and compacted to the first reinforcement level, usually to 95 to 100 percent of AASHTO T 99 maximum density within the specified moisture range, preferably a few percent dry of optimum. Uniform loose lift thickness should not exceed 12 inches; generally an 8-inch compacted lift is used. Fill is dumped toward the rear and middle of the reinforcement and bladed toward the face; retained backfill follows to the same elevation. Reinforcement is placed and connected when the fill is at or just above the connection (no gap, to avoid downdrag on the connection), generally perpendicular to the facing. The steps are repeated for each layer, then traffic barriers and copings are built.
key_points: Leveling pad: unreinforced 6-in. concrete, not a structural foundation.
Compaction: 95 to 100% of AASHTO T 99, a few percent dry of optimum.
Loose lift not over 12 in.; 8-in. compacted lift typical.
Connect reinforcement with fill at or just above the connection to avoid downdrag.
sections.applicability: Applies to field construction sequence and compaction control of MSE walls.

sections.title: Wall Facings
sections.summary: MSE facing types: segmental precast panels (minimum 5-1/2 in. thick, typically 5 ft by 5 or 10 ft), dry cast MBW units (30-110 lb, typically 8 in. high, 18 in. face, 12 in. deep), welded wire mesh, gabions, geosynthetic wrap-around (needs UV stabilization) and post-construction facings (pp. 10-32 to 10-33).
sections.body: Facings control aesthetics as the only visible part, protect against backfill sloughing and erosion, provide drainage paths in some cases, and influence settlement tolerance (p. 10-32). Segmental precast concrete panels: minimum thickness 5-1/2 inches or greater; square, rectangular, cruciform, diamond or hexagonal; typical nominal size 5 feet high and 5 or 10 feet wide; temperature and tensile reinforcement designed per Section 5 of AASHTO (2014). Dry cast modular block wall (MBW) units: small concrete units weighing 30 to 110 pounds, with 75 to 110 pounds routinely used for highways; unit height typically 8 inches (range 4 to 15); exposed face length 8 to 18 inches, 18 typical; front-to-back width typically 12 inches (range 8 to 24); solid or with cores filled with aggregate; dry-stacked in running bond and connected by pins, lips or keys (p. 10-33). Welded wire mesh: grid bent up at the face, possibly continuous with the reinforcement; galvanized for permanent and black steel for temporary walls. Gabion facing: rock-filled wire baskets with WWM, geogrid, geotextile or double-twisted woven mesh reinforcement. Geosynthetic facing: reinforcement looped around at the face, smooth or stepped; must be UV stabilized; vegetation through geogrids protects and improves appearance. Post-construction facing: shotcrete, cast-in-place concrete or attached panels added after construction, at added cost, useful where large differential settlement is expected.
key_points: Precast panels: at least 5-1/2 in. thick; typical 5 ft high by 5 or 10 ft wide.
MBW units: 30-110 lb (75-110 lb on highways), typically 8 in. high, 18 in. face, 12 in. deep.
Wrap-around geosynthetic faces must be UV stabilized.
Post-construction facings suit sites with large differential settlement.
sections.applicability: Use when selecting a facing type for an MSE wall.

sections.title: Soil Reinforcements
sections.summary: MSE reinforcements: galvanized steel strips (ribbed 2 in. by 5/32 in., or sine-wave), welded wire grids (W7.5-W24 longitudinal at 6 or 8 in., W11-W20 transverse at 6-24 in.), double-twisted PVC-coated mesh, HDPE and PVC-coated PET geogrids, PET and PP geotextiles, geosynthetic straps and geocomposites (pp. 10-34 to 10-35).
sections.body: Steel and geosynthetic reinforcements are used; steel is generally hot dip galvanized after fabrication (p. 10-34). Steel strips: ribbed top and bottom, 2 inches wide and 5/32-inch thick, or a 1/4-inch high sine-wave shape 1-1/2, 2 or 2-1/2 inches wide and 5/32-inch thick; smooth strips 2 to 4-3/4 inches wide and 1/8 to 5/32-inch thick have been used; used with segmental precast panels. Steel grids: welded wire grid with two to six W7.5 to W24 longitudinal wires at 6 or 8 inches and W11 to W20 transverse wires at 6 to 24 inches; 2 by 2-inch mesh of thinner wire has been used with welded wire facing; two-wire grids are ladder grids, used with precast panel, MBW and steel grid facings. Double twisted steel mesh: a proprietary galvanized, PVC-coated mesh used with gabion faced walls. HDPE geogrid: uniaxial, various strength grades, used with precast panel, MBW, WWM and wrap-around facings. PVC coated PET geogrid: bundled high tenacity PET fibers in the load direction, used with MBW, large precast block and wrap-around facings. High strength geotextiles: PET and PP, used with wrap-around and MBW facings. Geosynthetic strap: PET fibers in a PE sheath, used with precast panel walls (p. 10-35). Geocomposites: geogrids or knitted and woven geotextiles combined with nonwoven geotextiles for drainage where poorly draining fills are used.
key_points: Steel strips: ribbed 2 in. wide by 5/32 in. thick, or sine-wave strips.
Steel grids: W7.5-W24 longitudinal at 6 or 8 in.; W11-W20 transverse at 6-24 in.
Geosynthetics: HDPE geogrid, PVC-coated PET geogrid, PET/PP geotextile, PET strap in PE sheath.
Geocomposites add drainage with poorly draining fills.
sections.applicability: Use to match reinforcement types to MSE wall facing types.

sections.title: Reinforced Soil Fill
sections.summary: MSE select granular fill: Table 10-5 gradation (100% passing 4 in., 0-60% No. 40, 0-15% No. 200; Cu at least 4 for default F*), friction angle over 34 degrees, PI under 6, soundness loss under 30%; electrochemical limits for steel and geosynthetics; GRS-IBS open-graded fill at 38 degrees, AASHTO No. 8 or No. 89 (pp. 10-35 to 10-37).
sections.body: MSE walls require high quality, well graded granular fill, reasonably free of organic or deleterious material, conforming to Table 10-5 (p. 10-35): 100 percent passing 4 inches (102 mm), 0-60 percent passing No. 40 (0.425 mm), 0-15 percent passing No. 200 (0.075 mm); to apply default F* values Cu should be at least 4, and maximum particle size is reduced to 3/4 inch for geosynthetics and epoxy or PVC coated steel unless construction damage tests have been done. DOTs may adjust the broad range for local materials. Fill should be well graded per USCS (ASTM D2487). Table 10-6 (p. 10-36): angle of friction greater than 34 degrees (AASHTO T 236, on the portion finer than No. 10 compacted to 95% of T 99; no testing where 80% of sizes exceed 3/4 inch, using 34 degrees), PI less than 6 (AASHTO T 90), and magnesium sulfate soundness loss less than 30 percent after four cycles (AASHTO T 104). Table 10-7, steel reinforcement: resistivity greater than 3000 ohm-cm (T 288), pH greater than 5 and less than 10 (T 289), chlorides less than 100 ppm and sulfates less than 200 ppm (ASTM D4327), organic content 1 percent maximum (T 267). Table 10-8, geosynthetics: PET 3 < pH < 9; polyolefin (PP and HDPE) pH > 3 (T 289). High quality fill drains better, is more durable for steel and needs less reinforcement (pp. 10-36 to 10-37). GRS-IBS fill: minimum friction angle 38 degrees, typically open-graded crushed angular stone with 100 percent passing 3/4 inch and 0 to 5 percent passing No. 50; AASHTO M43 No. 8 (Table 10-9) and No. 89 (Table 10-10) meet this (p. 10-37).
key_points: Table 10-5: 100% passing 4 in.; 0-60% passing No. 40; 0-15% passing No. 200.
Table 10-6: phi > 34 deg; PI < 6; Mg sulfate soundness loss < 30% after four cycles.
Table 10-7 (steel): resistivity > 3000 ohm-cm; 5 < pH < 10; chlorides < 100 ppm; sulfates < 200 ppm; organics 1% max.
Table 10-8: PET 3 < pH < 9; PP and HDPE pH > 3.
GRS-IBS: phi at least 38 deg; open-graded AASHTO No. 8 or No. 89.

sections.title: Appurtenant Materials
sections.summary: Precast panel walls need compressible bearing pads (EPDM rubber or HDPE) in horizontal joints sized to wall height and geotextile filter strips over all joints; MBW walls use a gravel zone usually 1 ft wide behind and within the units with a soil or geotextile filter (p. 10-38).
sections.body: Walls with precast concrete panels need bearing pads in their horizontal joints to give some compressibility and movement between panels during elastic compression and settlement of the reinforced fill, mitigating downdrag stress on the reinforcement-facing connection and preventing concrete-to-concrete contact (p. 10-38). Pads are generally EPDM rubber or HDPE, with compressibility and thickness a function of wall height. All panel joints are covered on the back face with geotextile filter strips that prevent migration of fines and allow free drainage; the geotextile AOS and permeability must be compatible with the fill gradation. Bearing pads are not routinely used with MBW units. A zone of aggregate fill, usually 1-foot wide, is used behind the MBW units and within cored units; a soil or geotextile filter, properly designed for gradation, AOS and permeability, is required between the gravel and the wall fill.
key_points: Bearing pads (EPDM rubber or HDPE) in panel joints; sized to wall height.
Geotextile filter strips behind all panel joints.
MBW walls: aggregate zone usually 1 ft wide plus a filter.
sections.applicability: Use when detailing joints, bearing pads and drainage aggregate for MSE wall facings.

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Heading for MSE wall construction specifications and quality assurance: specification development, quality assurance with the field inspection checklist of Table 10-11, and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (pp. 10-38 to 10-41).
sections.body: Section 3.4 (p. 10-38) gives an overview of MSE wall construction specifications and quality assurance: specification development (3.4.1), a summary of quality assurance with the field inspection checklist of Table 10-11 (3.4.2), and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (3.4.3).
sections.applicability: Entry point for contracting, inspection and monitoring of MSE walls.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: MSE walls are contracted either by a performance (end-result) approach using approved systems with lines and grades and design criteria, or by agency design with components and execution fully specified (e.g., standard designs); most agencies prefer performance specifications, except for GRS-IBS abutments (p. 10-38).
sections.body: MSE wall systems are contracted by two approaches (p. 10-38): (1) a performance or end-result approach using approved systems and components, with lines and grades on the drawings and geometric and design criteria specified, and a project-specific design review and detail plan submittal with the working drawings; and (2) agency designs with system components, drainage details, erosion measures and construction execution explicitly specified in the contract documents, which can use standard designs for common wall heights (e.g., Minnesota DOT 2016). Both are valid if properly implemented and each has advantages and disadvantages. Most agencies prefer the performance-based specification for MSE walls; an exception is GRS-IBS abutments, which agencies typically design and specify themselves.
key_points: Two approaches: performance/end-result with approved systems, or agency design.
Most agencies prefer performance specifications; GRS-IBS usually agency designed.
sections.applicability: Applies to choosing a contracting approach for MSE walls.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: MSE construction is simple and rapid but attention to detail is essential; suppliers and inspectors should be trained. Table 10-11 outlines the field inspection checklist: specifications, plans, submittals, site and foundation, precast unit rejection criteria, labels, sampling, installation, damage checks and facing alignment (pp. 10-39 to 10-41).
sections.body: MSE construction mainly consists of preparing the subgrade, placing and compacting backfill in normal lifts, laying reinforcement and installing facing (p. 10-39). Special skills or equipment are usually not required and local labor can be used, but attention to detail is essential for performance and aesthetics, and experienced crews give higher production. Suppliers provide training, and training should also be required for those monitoring construction. Table 10-11 (pp. 10-39 to 10-40, source GEC 11) outlines general inspection requirements for MSE and RSS, to be expanded by the agency: (1) read the specifications (materials, procedures, compaction, tolerances, acceptance criteria); (2) review plans (sequence, corrosion protection, damage-reducing placement, compaction restrictions, drainage and utility details, slope face, contractor documents); (3) review material requirements, submittals and construction sequence; (4) check site and foundation conditions (foundation preparation, leveling pad level and alignment, access, excavation limits, dewatering, drainage features); (5) check reinforcements and prefabricated units, rejecting precast facing for low compressive strength, molding defects, honeycombing, severe cracking, chipping or spalling, color variation, tolerance or misaligned connections; (6) check labels against certifications; (7) check batch uniformity; (8) obtain test samples; (9) observe installation; (10) check for installation damage, e.g., by trial installation; (11) check against the approved shipment; (12) monitor facing alignment and line and grade. Special considerations for system type, site, fill and facing should be addressed in preconstruction reviews and inspection (pp. 10-40 to 10-41).
key_points: Training should be required for construction monitoring personnel.
Reject precast facing for strength, molding defects, honeycombing, cracking, color, tolerance or misaligned connections.
Check reinforcement for installation damage, e.g., with a trial installation.
tables: Table 10-11: Outline of MSE Wall Field Inspection Checklist Requirements (pp. 10-39 to 10-40)
sections.applicability: Use when preparing inspection and QA procedures for MSE walls and RSS.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Extensive MSE wall monitoring is needed only for new features or materials, large post-construction settlement, rate control, reinforcement degradation monitoring or asset management; a minimum program (as-built drawings, a few survey points) is advised for all walls. Agency-specific erection manuals guide control (p. 10-41).
sections.body: Because MSE wall technology is well established, extensive monitoring should be limited to projects with new features or materials, substantial anticipated post-construction settlement and/or construction rates needing control, monitoring of reinforcement degradation or corrosion (e.g., to allow marginal fills), or asset management (p. 10-41). A minimum monitoring program should be established for all structures for asset management, which could be as-built drawings with a few survey points at the top and bottom of the structure at select locations (critical features, tallest section). Where a monitoring program is used, first define the purpose; every instrument should answer a specific question, and if there is no question there should be no instrumentation. Each construction step is controlled by method requirements and tolerances. Construction manuals for proprietary systems should be obtained from the contractor, should be agency-specific rather than generic, and should be required when a system is placed on an approved products list. See GEC 11 and Section 3.3 for construction steps and controls.
key_points: Minimum program for all walls: as-built drawings plus a few top and bottom survey points.
Extensive monitoring only for new features, large settlement, rate control, degradation or asset management.
Require agency-specific erection manuals for approved systems.
sections.applicability: Applies to planning monitoring and construction control for MSE walls.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: MSE wall costs depend on cut-fill, size, soil, fill availability, facing and permanence; precast-faced MSE walls are usually cheaper than reinforced concrete walls above about 10 ft; savings of about 25 to 50 percent; typical permanent wall costs $30 to $65 per square foot of face (pp. 10-41 to 10-42).
sections.body: Site specific costs depend on cut-fill requirements, wall/slope size and type, in situ soil, available fill and backfill, facing finish, and temporary or permanent use (p. 10-41). MSE walls with precast concrete facings are usually less expensive than reinforced concrete retaining walls for heights greater than about 10 feet and average foundation conditions; MBW faced walls are competitive with concrete walls at all heights and for small projects (p. 10-42). In general, MSE walls give savings on the order of 25 to 50 percent and possibly more compared with a conventional reinforced concrete retaining structure, especially one on deep foundations, largely by eliminating deep foundations because reinforced soil tolerates relatively large total and differential settlements; ease and speed of construction also save cost. Typical total costs for permanent transportation MSE walls range from $30 to $65 per square foot of face, varying with height, project size, aesthetic treatment, site access and cost of select fill; regional fill costs may make costs much higher.
key_points: Precast-faced MSE walls usually cheaper than RC walls above about 10 ft.
Savings about 25 to 50 percent versus conventional RC walls.
Typical permanent wall cost: $30 to $65 per square foot of face.
sections.applicability: Use for preliminary cost comparison of MSE walls with conventional walls.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Relative costs for precast-faced MSE walls: erection and profit 20-30%, reinforcement 15-30%, facing 20-40%, reinforced fill 30-60%; architectural finish $0.50-$1.50 per sq ft; traffic barrier about $170 per linear ft; MBW walls under 15 ft are typically at least 10% cheaper (p. 10-42).
sections.body: The cost of a specific MSEW structure depends on its principal components (p. 10-42). For segmental precast concrete faced structures, typical relative costs are: erection of panels and contractor's profit, 20 to 30 percent of total cost; reinforcing materials, 15 to 30 percent; facing system, 20 to 40 percent; and reinforced wall fill including placement, 30 to 60 percent where the fill is select granular fill from an off-site borrow source. Additional cost for panel architectural finish treatment ranges from $0.50 to $1.50 per square foot depending on complexity. Traffic barrier costs average $170 per linear foot. Excavation cost may be somewhat greater than for other systems because of the reinforcement zone width. MBW faced walls less than 15 feet high are typically less expensive than segmental panel faced walls by 10 percent or more.
key_points: Erection and profit 20-30%; reinforcement 15-30%; facing 20-40%; fill 30-60%.
Architectural finish $0.50 to $1.50/sq ft; traffic barrier about $170/linear ft.
MBW walls under 15 ft: at least 10% cheaper than panel walls.
sections.applicability: Applies to breaking down and estimating MSE wall costs.

sections.title: Reinforced Soil Slopes
sections.summary: Section heading for reinforced soil slopes (RSS): feasibility considerations, construction and materials, design overview, construction specifications and quality assurance, and cost data (pp. 10-43 to 10-58).
sections.body: Section 4.0 (p. 10-43) covers reinforced soil slopes: feasibility considerations (4.1), construction and materials (4.2), design overview (4.3), specifications and quality assurance (4.4) and cost data (4.5).
sections.applicability: Entry point for reinforced soil slopes on firm foundations.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: RSS are MSE structures with planar reinforcement (typically geosynthetics) in constructed earth slopes with face inclinations less than 70 degrees; they are cost-effective for new construction and reconstruction where fill, right-of-way or other costs make a steeper slope desirable (p. 10-43).
sections.body: Reinforced soil slopes (RSS) are a form of mechanically stabilized earth that incorporate planar reinforcing elements (typically geosynthetics) in constructed earth sloped structures with face inclinations of less than 70 degrees (p. 10-43). Multiple layers of reinforcement are placed during construction or reconstruction to reinforce the soil and increase stability. RSS structures are cost-effective alternatives for new construction and reconstruction where the cost of fill, right-of-way and other considerations may make a steeper slope desirable.
key_points: RSS face inclination is less than 70 degrees.
Typically geosynthetic reinforcement.
sections.applicability: Applies to screening steepened reinforced slopes against flatter slopes or walls.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: RSS allow embankments steeper than the soil alone permits: steepened slopes on firm foundations, road widening within right-of-way, and repair of failed slopes reusing slide debris; also shorter bridge spans, temporary detours, preventing surface sloughing, wet fine-grained fills, levees and flood control (pp. 10-43 to 10-44).
sections.body: Reinforcement is used to construct an embankment steeper than could otherwise be safely built with the same soil (p. 10-43). The increased stability allows steepened slopes on firm foundations for new highways, as an alternative to flatter unreinforced slopes and to retaining walls. Roadways can be widened over existing flatter slopes without encroaching beyond existing right-of-way. RSS can also repair a failed slope, usually reusing the slide debris as reinforced fill, giving a safer slope and possibly substantial savings over importing higher quality backfill. These applications are illustrated in Figure 10-9. Other applications have included decreased bridge spans, temporary road widening for detours, prevention of surface sloughing during saturation, embankment construction with wet fine-grained soils, permanent levees and temporary flood control structures.
key_points: Steepened slopes on firm foundations; road widening within ROW.
Slope repair reusing slide debris.
Also bridge span reduction, detours, sloughing prevention, wet fine-grained fills, levees.
sections.applicability: Use to identify where reinforced soil slopes fit highway projects.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (10.4.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (10.4.1.2.2, printed 2.1.2.2) of reinforced soil slopes.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of RSS, 10.4.1.2.1 and 10.4.1.2.2 (printed 2.1.2.2); it has no text of its own. (p. 10-44)
sections.applicability: Use when comparing RSS with flatter slopes or retaining walls.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Steeper RSS save material and right-of-way and may reuse lower-quality fill such as slide debris; they can cost about half as much as MSE walls; vegetated faces blend in; with inherent conservatism they are safer than flatter unreinforced slopes at the same factor of safety.
sections.body: Economic advantages of a safe, steeper RSS come from material and right-of-way savings, and lower quality material may serve, e.g., reusing slide debris in landslide repair. Right-of-way savings can be substantial, especially for urban widenings where new right-of-way is costly or unobtainable. RSS are also an economical alternative to retaining walls, in some cases at about one-half the cost of MSE walls. Vegetated faces can blend with natural settings, though maintenance (e.g., mowing) must be handled in design. With inherent design conservatism and reinforcement strength more reliable than soil strength, RSS are actually safer than flatter unreinforced slopes at the same factor of safety (p. 10-45), with less risk of the long-term problems common in fill slopes built to low factors of safety or with marginal materials (shale, low cohesion silts, plastic soils). (pp. 10-44 to 10-45)
key_points: Material and right-of-way savings; slide debris reuse (p. 10-44).
In some cases about one-half the cost of MSE walls (p. 10-44).
Safer than flatter unreinforced slopes at the same factor of safety (p. 10-44).
sections.applicability: Use when comparing RSS with flatter slopes or retaining walls.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Printed 2.1.2.2. Like all reinforced soil structures, RSS need a relatively large space behind the face for reinforcement, and an end-result specification shares design responsibility between suppliers and owners.
sections.body: Printed with the number 2.1.2.2 under 4.1.2, as printed. General potential disadvantages of reinforced soil structures, depending on local and project conditions: a relatively large space (e.g., excavation in a cut) behind the slope face for reinforcement; and, with an end result RSS specification, design responsibility shared between system/material suppliers and owners. (p. 10-45)
key_points: Large space behind the face for reinforcement (p. 10-45).
End result specification shares design responsibility (p. 10-45).
sections.applicability: Use when comparing RSS with flatter slopes or retaining walls.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental, site and aesthetic feasibility of reinforced soil slopes (10.4.1.3.1 to 10.4.1.3.4).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of RSS, 10.4.1.3.1 to 10.4.1.3.4; it has no text of its own. (p. 10-45)
sections.applicability: Applies to screening a site and environment for a reinforced soil slope.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: An adequate foundation investigation is key, since missed soft soils cause differential settlement; establish bearing resistance, global stability, settlement and groundwater.
sections.body: An adequate subsurface investigation of the foundation is key; distress is often traced to exploration that missed soft soils, causing local differential settlement. Foundation properties should establish bearing resistance, global stability, settlement potential and groundwater levels. (p. 10-45)
key_points: Establish bearing, global stability, settlement and groundwater (p. 10-45).
sections.applicability: Applies to screening a site and environment for a reinforced soil slope.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Erosion control and revegetation must be part of every RSS design, not left to the contractor. Ground aggressiveness governs reinforcement: PET degrades at high or low pH (e.g., lime-treated soil), polyolefins in acidic metal-bearing soil; steel corrodes faster above about 200 ppm chlorides/sulfates or pH < 5; pH > 10 strips galvanizing.
sections.body: Runoff erosion threatens slope stability, so erosion control and revegetation must be integral to every reinforced slope design and specification; unprotected slopes should be vegetated after construction. Vegetation is project specific, slope face protection should not be left to the contractor or vendor, and maintenance and landscaping groups should advise on low maintenance vegetation. The aggressiveness of the reinforced fill, retained backfill and natural soils governs reinforcement type and performance, including later deicing salts or fertilizers (p. 10-46). Polyester (PET) degrades in highly alkaline or acidic ground (e.g., lime stabilized soils); polyolefins only in certain highly acidic, metal-bearing soils (e.g., ferric soils, mine waste) (FHWA 2009). For steel, chlorides and sulfates generally above 200 ppm and pH less than 5 accelerate corrosion; pH > 10 accelerates loss of galvanization. (pp. 10-45 to 10-46)
key_points: Erosion control and revegetation integral to design (p. 10-45).
PET degrades at high or low pH, e.g., lime-treated soils (p. 10-46).
Steel: chlorides/sulfates above about 200 ppm or pH < 5 (p. 10-46).
sections.applicability: Applies to screening a site and environment for a reinforced soil slope.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: RSS suit fill-type construction and side-hill fills, where excavation is small; large cuts reduce but often do not remove the economy.
sections.body: RSS structures are particularly well suited where a 'fill-type' wall must be built or side-hill fills are indicated, where excavation may be small and the economy is kept; large cut volumes diminish it but in many cases it remains viable. (p. 10-46)
key_points: Suited to fill-type construction and side-hill fills (p. 10-46).
sections.applicability: Applies to screening a site and environment for a reinforced soil slope.

sections.title: Aesthetics
sections.summary: RSS faces about 1:1 or flatter are usually vegetated; steeper faces can be vegetated with a stepped face for runoff, or use soil bioengineered or hard armor facing (GEC 11).
sections.body: RSS faces of about 1:1 or flatter are usually vegetated, with project specific requirements by geography and climate. Steeper slopes may be vegetated with a stepped facing to control runoff; slopes steeper than about 1:1 may also use a soil bioengineered or hard armor facing (see GEC 11). (p. 10-46)
key_points: Faces about 1:1 or flatter usually vegetated (p. 10-46).
sections.applicability: Applies to screening a site and environment for a reinforced soil slope.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: RSS design often assumes a firm foundation; steepening increases bearing failure risk over soft soils and needs extensive exploration and rigorous analysis. Design charts do not cover basal reinforcement over soft soils, for which FHWA (2008a) applies (pp. 10-46 to 10-47).
sections.body: The design of RSS structures often assumes a stable or firm foundation (p. 10-46). Steepening a slope significantly increases the potential for bearing capacity failure over soft soils, so extensive geotechnical exploration and rigorous analysis are required. Design charts and some design procedures do not address reinforcing the base of a reinforced slope built over soft soils, which is a different reinforcement application; the FHWA Geosynthetics Design and Construction Guidelines (FHWA 2008a) cover that application (p. 10-47). An extension is to lengthen reinforcement at the base of the embankment to improve global stability of a reinforced soil slope.
key_points: RSS design usually assumes a firm foundation.
Over soft soils, basal reinforcement is a separate application (FHWA 2008a).
sections.applicability: Use to check whether foundation conditions fall outside standard RSS design.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions
sections.summary: Alternatives to RSS: MSE walls, cantilever, gravity, semi-gravity or counterfort concrete walls, or soil embankments. RSS may be cost effective in rural areas with ROW limits or long sliver fills, and in urban areas where ROW is available, being generally cheaper than vertical MSE walls (p. 10-47).
sections.body: MSE walls; cantilever, gravity, semi gravity or counterfort concrete walls; or soil embankments are the usual alternatives to an RSS structure (p. 10-47). RSS may be cost effective in rural environments where right-of-way restrictions exist, or on widening projects where long sliver fills are necessary. In urban environments they should be considered where right-of-way is available, as they are generally more economical than vertically faced MSE wall structures.
key_points: Alternatives: MSE walls, concrete walls, soil embankments.
Generally more economical than vertically faced MSE walls where ROW allows.
sections.applicability: Applies to choosing between RSS and wall or embankment alternatives.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: General RSS construction requirements are in GEC 11; RSS may be specified as a vendor-designed system from an approved products list with an agency-specific erection manual, or designed in-house by the agency with material and construction specifications (p. 10-47).
sections.body: General construction requirements and guidance for RSSs are in GEC 11 (p. 10-47). As discussed in Section 4.4, RSSs may be specified as a system with vendor design and an approved products (RSS system) list established by the DOT, in which case a system- and agency-specific construction erection manual should be required from each vendor and used by the contractor, inspectors and agency. Alternatively, RSSs may be designed in-house by an agency, with material and construction specifications. The reinforcement and facing materials are summarized in this section; see GEC 11 for detail.
key_points: Vendor-designed system with approved products list, or in-house agency design.
sections.applicability: Entry point for RSS construction sequence, facing, reinforcement and fill.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: RSS construction resembles normal slope construction: place soil, place reinforcement, construct face. Sequence: site preparation and drains; reinforcement perpendicular to the face, pinned, 6-in. edge overlap for wrapped faces; at least 6 in. of fill under equipment; compaction to 95% of T 99 within 2% of optimum; face construction (pp. 10-47 to 10-49).
sections.body: Construction of reinforced slopes is very similar to normal slope construction because reinforcement layers are easily placed between compacted lifts; the elements are placing the soil, placing the reinforcement and constructing the face (p. 10-47). The usual sequence (GEC 11, pp. 10-47 to 10-49): Site preparation: clear and grub; remove slide debris for reinstatement; prepare a level subgrade; proof-roll the base and test as required; observe and approve the foundation; place drainage features (basedrain and/or backdrain). Reinforcing layer placement: principal strength direction perpendicular to the slope face; secure with retaining pins; a minimum overlap of 6 inches along edges perpendicular to the slope for wrapped faces, or clipped or tied grid edges; butted edges where reinforcement is not needed for face support. Reinforced fill placement: place fill with a loader or dozer operating on placed fill or natural ground; keep at least 6 inches of fill between reinforcement and wheels or tracks; compact with vibratory roller or plate compactor (granular) or rubber-tired or smooth drum roller (cohesive); avoid moving the reinforcement; use lightweight compaction near wrapped and welded wire faces. Compaction control: at least 95 percent of standard AASHTO T 99 maximum density within 2 percent of optimum moisture; for coarse aggregate, a relative density or method specification. Face construction depends on soil type, slope angle and reinforcement spacing.
key_points: Reinforcement strength direction perpendicular to the face; pinned in place.
Minimum 6-in. edge overlap for wrapped faces; at least 6 in. of fill under equipment.
Compaction: at least 95% of AASHTO T 99 within 2% of optimum moisture.
sections.applicability: Applies to field construction of reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: RSS Facing
sections.summary: RSS facings prevent sloughing and erosion: no wrap may be needed up to about 1H:1V; reinforcement spacing for wrapped or unwrapped faces no greater than 16 in., and generally no greater than 32 in. or the facing width for hard faces. Facings are soft vegetated or hard; Figure 10-10 shows smooth, wrapped and stepped faces (pp. 10-49 to 10-50).
sections.body: Facing is needed where the slope angle exceeds the soil friction strength (to prevent sloughing) or for erosion (p. 10-49). Wrapped faces can be formed with sufficient reinforcement length; a face wrap may not be required for slopes up to about 1H:1V, where primary and secondary reinforcements are simply extended to the face. Face compaction is by running equipment over and down the face or by overbuilding and cutting back to the reinforcement; for the no-wrap option, a facing treatment is applied at intervals during construction to prevent erosion. For wrapped or no-wrap construction the reinforcement is kept at close spacing (every lift or every other lift, but no greater than 16 inches); for armored, hard faced systems the maximum spacing should generally be no greater than 32 inches or the width of the facing. The outward slope is covered with a protective facing that limits erosion, protects the reinforcement and gives surficial stability; facings are soft vegetated or hard, including wrapped reinforcement, welded wire forms, gabions and concrete units. Hard facings and wraps become necessary with steeper slopes and more erodible soils. Living vegetation (grasses, small woody plants) aids aesthetics and erosion control and may add tensile strength. Wrapped faces give more lateral confinement near the face; non-wrapped faces suit gentle slopes. Typical face geometries are in Figure 10-10 (Brickman and Berg 2013).
key_points: Face wrap may be unnecessary for slopes up to about 1H:1V.
Reinforcement spacing for wrapped or unwrapped faces: no greater than 16 in.
Hard faced systems: maximum spacing generally 32 in. or the facing width.
Facings are soft (vegetated) or hard; wraps confine the face.
figures: Figure 10-10: RSS face geometries - smooth, wrapped, and stepped. (Brickman and Berg 2013; p. 10-50)
sections.applicability: Use when selecting and detailing the facing of a reinforced soil slope.

sections.title: Soil Reinforcements
sections.summary: RSS reinforcements: HDPE geogrid and PVC-coated PET geogrid (WWM-faced, wrap-around and non-wrap faces), PET and PP geotextiles (wrap-around, may be shotcreted), welded wire steel grids (W7.5-W24 longitudinal at 6 or 8 in.) and proprietary double-twisted PVC-coated steel mesh with gabion faces (pp. 10-50 to 10-51).
sections.body: Geosynthetic and steel reinforcements are used with RSSs (p. 10-50). HDPE geogrid: uniaxial, in various strength grades, used with WWM faced, wrap-around and non-wrap slope facings. PVC coated PET geogrid: from several manufacturers in various grades, with bundled high tenacity PET fibers in the load direction; used with WWM faced, wrap-around and non-wrap facings. High strength geotextiles: PET and PP, used with wrap-around faces and may be coated with shotcrete or other material for permanent slopes (pp. 10-50 to 10-51). Steel grids: welded wire grid with W7.5 to W24 longitudinal wire at 6 or 8 inches and W11 to W20 transverse wire at 6 to 24 inches, generally used with steel grid slope facings; 2 by 2-inch mesh of thinner wire has been used with welded wire facing. Double twisted steel mesh: a proprietary galvanized, PVC-coated soft-tempered mesh generally used with an integral double twisted mesh gabion face.
key_points: HDPE and PVC-coated PET geogrids for WWM, wrap-around and non-wrap faces.
Geotextiles for wrap-around faces, possibly shotcreted for permanent slopes.
Steel grids: W7.5-W24 longitudinal at 6 or 8 in.; W11-W20 transverse at 6-24 in.
sections.applicability: Use to match RSS reinforcement types to slope facing types.

sections.title: Reinforced Soil Fill
sections.summary: RSS fill is less stringent than MSE fill: Table 10-12 gradation (100% passing 4 in., 100-20% No. 4, 0-60% No. 40, 0-50% No. 200), Table 10-13 PI 20 or less and soundness loss under 30%; electrochemical limits of Tables 10-7 and 10-8; compaction 95% of T 99 within 2% of optimum (pp. 10-51 to 10-52).
sections.body: RSS reinforced fill requirements are less stringent than for MSE walls (Section 3.3.4), since facings are typically flexible and tolerate some distortion, but a high quality embankment fill is still recommended to ease compaction and minimize reinforcement (p. 10-51). Fill should be reasonably free of organic or deleterious material. Table 10-12 (p. 10-52) recommends: 100 percent passing 4 inches (102 mm); 100 to 20 percent passing No. 4 (4.76 mm); 0 to 60 percent passing No. 40 (0.425 mm); 0 to 50 percent passing No. 200 (0.075 mm); Cu at least 4 to apply default F* values, and maximum particle size reduced to 3/4 inch for geosynthetics and epoxy or PVC coated steel unless construction damage tests have been done. DOTs may adjust the range. Fills with steel reinforcement must meet Table 10-7 and with geosynthetics Table 10-8. Table 10-13: PI 20 or less (AASHTO T 90) and magnesium sulfate soundness loss less than 30 percent after four cycles (AASHTO T 104). Fills outside these limits have been used both successfully and unsuccessfully; drainage, distortion and settlement must be evaluated carefully for finer or more plastic soils. Compaction should be based on 95 percent of AASHTO T 99 and plus or minus 2 percent of optimum moisture (p. 10-51).
key_points: Table 10-13: PI 20 or less; Mg sulfate soundness loss < 30% after four cycles.
Compaction: 95% of AASHTO T 99, within plus or minus 2% of optimum.

Notes: a. To apply default F* values, Cu, should be greater than or equal to 4. b. The maximum particle size for these materials should be reduced to ¾-inch for geosynthetics, and for epoxy and PVC coated steel reinforcements unless construction damage assessment tests are or have been performed on the reinforcement combination with the specific or similarly graded large size granular fill.

The material shall have a magnesium sulfate soundness loss of less than 30 percent after four cycles.
sections.applicability: Applies to specifying reinforced fill for reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: RSS reinforcement serves stability of steepened slopes and repairs, or as a compaction aid. Design uses limit equilibrium, allowable stress with adequate factors of safety short and long term; LRFD is not developed for slopes. Three failure modes: internal, external and compound (Figure 10-11) (pp. 10-52 to 10-53).
sections.body: There are two main purposes for reinforcement in slopes (p. 10-52): improved stability for steepened slopes and slope repair; and compaction aids, for support of construction equipment and improved face stability. Design of reinforcement for safe, steep slopes requires rigorous analysis, as failure of the reinforcement would result in failure of the slope. The overall requirements are similar to unreinforced slopes: a limit equilibrium, allowable stress approach is used, and the factor of safety must be adequate for both short-term and long-term conditions and all possible failure modes. LRFD methods have not been fully developed for unreinforced or reinforced slopes and are not included in the manual (p. 10-53). As illustrated in Figure 10-11, there are three failure modes: internal, where the failure plane passes through the reinforcing elements; external, where the failure surface passes behind and underneath the reinforced zone; and compound, where the failure surface passes behind and through the reinforced zone. In some cases the calculated factor of safety can be approximately equal in two or all three modes if reinforcement strengths, lengths and spacing are optimized (Berg et al. 1989).
key_points: Limit equilibrium, allowable stress design; LRFD not developed for slopes.
Failure modes: internal, external, compound.
Optimized layouts can give nearly equal factors of safety in all modes (Berg et al. 1989).
figures: Figure 10-11: Failure modes for reinforced soil slope. (p. 10-53)
sections.applicability: Applies to the design basis and failure modes of reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: RSS stability uses conventional procedures and software modified for reinforcement; unlike basal embankment reinforcement, RSS reinforcement carries tension for the structure's life; facing design is critical and vegetated faces need maintenance. RSS may be designed in-house or by line-and-grade with shared responsibility (pp. 10-53 to 10-54).
sections.body: Stability calculations use conventional geotechnical procedures and design software, modified only for the reinforcement (p. 10-53). Unlike a reinforced embankment on soft soils, the reinforcement in RSS carries tensile load over the life of the structure, as in MSE walls. The facing system is a key component and its design is critical to performance; unlike MSE wall facings, a vegetated RSS face requires maintenance (water, fertilizer, cutting), which must be factored into facing selection and design. RSS may be designed in-house by an agency or by a line-and-grade approach like MSE walls. In-house, agency engineers select, specify and detail the reinforcement, facing and drainage and perform the stability analyses with reasonable soil properties and safety factors. With line-and-grade, design responsibility is shared between material suppliers and the agency specifier/owner (pp. 10-53 to 10-54).
key_points: RSS reinforcement carries tension for the life of the structure.
Vegetated faces need maintenance, which affects facing selection.
In-house agency design or line-and-grade with shared responsibility.
sections.applicability: Use when organizing the design of a reinforced soil slope.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: The basic RSS design steps for slopes on firm foundations are shown as a flow chart in Figure 10-12; steps vary with reinforcement type and complex RSSs need more; detailed guidance and examples are in GEC 11 (p. 10-54).
sections.body: The basic design steps for RSS structures are listed in Figure 10-12, a flow chart of steps for reinforced soil slope design (p. 10-54, from GEC 11). Some steps have several sub-steps. The steps are for RSSs on firm foundations; they can vary depending on the type of reinforcement and whether it is defined at the outset, and additional steps are required for more complex RSSs. Detailed design guidance, discussions, example calculations and steps for complex cases are in GEC 11. The chapter does not repeat the flow chart's individual steps in its text.
key_points: Design steps shown as a flow chart (Figure 10-12) for RSS on firm foundations.
Detailed steps and examples: GEC 11.
figures: Figure 10-12: Flow chart of steps for reinforced soil slope design. (GEC 11; p. 10-54)
sections.applicability: Applies to the design sequence for reinforced soil slopes on firm foundations.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: The primary reference for RSS design in transportation works is GEC 11 (2009), Design and Construction of Mechanically Stabilized Earth Walls and Reinforced Soil Slopes; Duncan and Wright (2005), Soil Strength and Slope Stability, is also very useful (p. 10-55).
sections.body: The primary reference for RSS design for transportation works is GEC 11 (2009), Design and Construction of Mechanically Stabilized Earth Walls and Reinforced Soil Slopes (Berg, Christopher and Samtani; FHWA NHI-10-024 Vol I and NHI-10-025 Vol II) (p. 10-55). Designers will also find Duncan and Wright (2005), Soil Strength and Slope Stability, very useful.
key_points: Primary: GEC 11 (2009).
Also useful: Duncan and Wright (2005).
sections.applicability: Use to locate detailed design guidance for reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Heading for RSS construction specifications and quality assurance: specification development, a summary of quality assurance, and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (pp. 10-55 to 10-57).
sections.body: Section 4.4 (p. 10-55) gives an overview of RSS construction specifications and quality assurance: specification development (4.4.1), a summary of quality assurance (4.4.2) and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (4.4.3).
sections.applicability: Entry point for contracting, inspection and monitoring of reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: RSS are contracted by a performance (end-result) approach with approved systems, where face vegetation requirements must be set by the specifier, or by agency design with components fully specified; many agencies prefer in-house design with a generic specification or standard designs (p. 10-55).
sections.body: RSS systems are contracted by two approaches (p. 10-55): a performance or end-result approach using approved systems and components, with lines and grades and geometric and design criteria specified and a project-specific design review with the working drawings, in which project-specific face vegetation protection requirements should be defined by the specifier and not left to the contractor or vendor; or agency designs with system components, drainage details, erosion measures and construction execution explicitly specified. Both are valid if properly implemented. Many agencies prefer to design in-house and use a generic specification for RSS components; agencies can also use standard designs for common slope heights (e.g., Minnesota DOT 2016).
key_points: Specifier must define face vegetation protection in end-result contracts.
Many agencies design RSS in-house with generic component specifications.
sections.applicability: Applies to choosing a contracting approach for reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: RSS construction is simple and rapid: subgrade, backfill lifts, reinforcement and face erosion protection, with local labor and supplier training. The Table 10-11 checklist applies, expanded by the agency; special considerations go into preconstruction reviews and inspection (pp. 10-55 to 10-56).
sections.body: Construction of RSS structures is relatively simple and rapid: preparing the subgrade, placing and compacting backfill in normal lifts, laying reinforcement and installing the facing erosion protection (p. 10-55). Special skills or equipment are usually not required, local labor can be used, and most suppliers provide training. The outline checklist for monitoring and inspecting MSE and RSS systems is Table 10-11, to be expanded by the agency with requirements from its specifications and the project plans (pp. 10-55 to 10-56). Special construction considerations relating to system type, site conditions, backfill and facing erosion protection should be addressed in preconstruction reviews, prefabricated materials inspection, construction control and/or performance monitoring; see GEC 11.
key_points: Use and expand the Table 10-11 inspection checklist for RSS.
sections.applicability: Use when planning inspection and QA for reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: RSS monitoring should be limited to new features or materials, large expected settlement, rate control or asset management; each instrument must answer a question. Construction steps: site preparation, subsurface drainage, reinforcement, fill, face, repeat, surface drainage (pp. 10-56 to 10-57).
sections.body: RSS technology is well established, so monitoring programs should be limited to designs with new features or materials, substantial anticipated post-construction settlement and/or construction rates requiring control, or asset management (p. 10-56). If monitoring is used, first define the purpose of the measurements; every instrument should help answer a specific question, and if there is no question there should be no instrumentation. Each construction step is controlled by method requirements and tolerances: for in-house designs they are detailed on the drawings and specifications; for end-result specifications, agency-specific construction manuals for the proprietary system should be obtained from the contractor and may be required to place the system on an approved products list. RSS construction is considerably simpler than MSE wall construction and consists of (pp. 10-56 to 10-57): site preparation; construct subsurface drainage features; place reinforcement layer; place and compact backfill on reinforcement; construct face; place additional reinforcement and fill; construct surface drainage features.
key_points: Monitoring only for new features, large settlement, rate control or asset management.
Construction steps: site prep, subsurface drainage, reinforcement, fill, face, repeat, surface drainage.
sections.applicability: Applies to monitoring and construction control of reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: RSS economy must be assessed case by case with a benefit-cost analysis of a steeper reinforced slope versus a flatter slope with more ROW and fill, including guardrails and erosion control. Bid prices about $10 to $24 per sq ft by height; about $16 per sq ft for 30- to 50-ft slopes (pp. 10-57 to 10-58).
sections.body: The economy of RSS must be assessed case by case where use is not dictated by space constraints, with a benefit-to-cost analysis of a steeper reinforced slope against a flatter slope with its added right-of-way and material costs (p. 10-57). Guardrails or traffic barriers are often needed for steeper slopes, and erosion control for face protection must be included. Factors to consider: cut or fill quantities; slope area size and average height; slope angle; cost of non-select versus select backfill; temporary and permanent erosion protection; cost and availability of right-of-way; complicated horizontal and vertical alignment changes; need for temporary excavation support; maintenance of traffic; aesthetics; and guardrail and barrier requirements. High RSS have relatively higher reinforcement and lower backfill costs (p. 10-58). Recent bid prices (GEC 11) suggest $10 to $24 per square foot as a function of height, and about $16 per square foot for the 30- to 50-foot height range, excluding safety features and drainage details.
key_points: Use a benefit-cost comparison against a flatter unreinforced slope.
Bid prices about $10 to $24/sq ft by height; about $16/sq ft for 30-50 ft slopes (GEC 11).
Prices exclude safety features and drainage details.
sections.applicability: Use for preliminary cost evaluation of reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Relative RSS costs from limited data: reinforcement 45 to 65 percent, reinforced fill 30 to 50 percent and face treatment 5 to 10 percent of total cost; compared with flatter slopes, the savings in soil alone often pay for the reinforcement (p. 10-58).
sections.body: The bid cost of a specific RSS depends on the cost of each of its principal components (p. 10-58). Based on limited data, typical relative costs are: reinforcement, 45 to 65 percent of total cost; reinforced fill, 30 to 50 percent; and face treatment, 5 to 10 percent. For RSS systems used as an alternate to flatter slopes, the savings in the soil alone will often pay for the reinforcement, as well as providing a more sustainable solution.
key_points: Reinforcement 45-65%; reinforced fill 30-50%; face treatment 5-10% of total cost.
sections.applicability: Applies to cost breakdowns for reinforced soil slopes.

sections.title: Soil Nail Walls
sections.summary: Section heading for soil nail walls: feasibility considerations, construction and materials, design overview, construction specifications and quality assurance, and cost data, with detailed guidance in GEC 7 (pp. 10-59 to 10-79).
sections.body: Section 5.0 (p. 10-59) covers soil nail walls built top-down: feasibility considerations (5.1), construction and materials (5.2), design overview (5.3), specifications and quality assurance (5.4) and cost data (5.5). Detailed guidance is in GEC 7.
sections.applicability: Entry point for soil nail walls for top-down excavation support and slope stabilization.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Soil nail walls are built top-down in excavation lifts of limited height with nails and initial shotcrete at each lift, then a final shotcrete or cast-in-place facing; they suit ground that can stand in short vertical or near-vertical cuts temporarily. GEC 7 discusses favorable conditions and cost factors (p. 10-59).
sections.body: Soil nail walls are constructed top-down: the ground is excavated in lifts of limited height and soil nails and an initial shotcrete facing are installed at each lift to provide support; a final shotcrete or cast-in-place concrete (CIP) facing is then installed (p. 10-59). Soil nail walls can be more advantageous than other top-down retaining systems where the ground can temporarily sustain short, vertical or sub-vertical unsupported cuts. GEC 7 discusses favorable and unfavorable subsurface conditions for cost-effective soil nailing, useful in evaluating feasibility, and the main factors affecting construction cost.
key_points: Top-down construction in limited-height lifts.
Requires ground that stands temporarily in short vertical or near-vertical cuts.
sections.applicability: Applies to screening soil nailing for an excavation or cut.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Soil nail wall applications: roadway cuts, road widening under existing bridge abutments, tunnel portals, repair of existing retaining structures, hybrid systems with anchors or MSE walls, shored MSE walls for low-volume roads in steep terrain, and temporary or permanent excavation support and slope stabilization (pp. 10-59 to 10-60).
sections.body: Soil nail walls can be used in the following roadway applications (pp. 10-59 to 10-60): roadway cuts, where only limited excavation and reasonable right-of-way and clearing limits are required; road widening under existing bridge abutments, where the small drill rig can work in limited overhead and underpass traffic may not need to be fully interrupted; tunnel portals, similar to road cuts with additional design and construction aspects; repair and reconstruction of existing retaining structures, stabilizing or strengthening failing or distressed structures; hybrid soil nail systems combined with ground anchor walls or MSE walls for complex layouts or where other systems are too costly; shored mechanically stabilized earth (SMSE) walls, combining permanent soil nail walls with MSE walls to limit excavation when widening low-volume roads in steep terrain (Section 6.2); and temporary and permanent excavation support and slope stabilization.
key_points: Roadway cuts; widening under bridge abutments; tunnel portals.
Repair of existing retaining structures; hybrid systems.
Shored MSE walls in steep terrain (Section 6.2).

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (10.5.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages or limitations (10.5.1.2.2) of soil nail walls.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of soil nail walls, 10.5.1.2.1 and 10.5.1.2.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 10-60)

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Soil nailing advantages (GEC 7): construction (small ROW, small equipment, fast, adjustable around obstructions, low headroom, curves); performance (flexible, tolerable deflections, good seismic record, more redundancy than anchored walls); cost (cheaper than gravity walls above about 12 to 15 ft, equal or cheaper than anchor walls).
sections.body: Advantages fall into construction, performance and cost (GEC 7). Construction: smaller ROW than most systems; less traffic disruption and environmental impact than drilled shafts or soldier piles; less congestion than braced excavations; relatively fast; nail inclination and location easily adjusted around boulders, piles or utilities; less restricted by overhead limits, important under bridges; small equipment for remote sites; multipurpose equipment; many qualified contractors and widespread knowledge; curves and bends easier than other top-down walls. Performance: relatively flexible, tolerating large total and differential movements; deflections usually within tolerable limits in roadway projects with proper control (p. 10-61); good seismic performance; more redundancy than anchored walls from more reinforcing elements per area; sculpted facings for a natural look. Cost: more economical than concrete gravity walls taller than about 12 to 15 feet, and equal to or more cost-effective than ground anchor walls with conventional procedures. (pp. 10-60 to 10-61)
key_points: Small ROW and equipment; adjustable around obstructions (p. 10-60).
More redundancy than anchored walls; good seismic record (p. 10-61).
Cheaper than gravity walls above about 12 to 15 ft (p. 10-61).
sections.applicability: Use when weighing soil nail walls against other top-down retaining systems.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages or Limitations
sections.summary: Strict movement criteria add cost or rule soil nails out; utilities behind the wall restrict nail location, inclination and length; large groundwater seepage is unsuitable; permanent walls need permanent underground easements (GEC 7).
sections.body: Main limitations or potential disadvantages (GEC 7): strict wall movement criteria may need extra measures and cost, and very strict criteria may make soil nails infeasible; utilities behind the wall will likely restrict nail location, inclination and length, especially in the upper rows; soil nail walls are not well suited where large amounts of groundwater seep into the excavation; and permanent walls need permanent underground easements. (p. 10-61)
key_points: Very strict movement criteria may rule soil nails out (p. 10-61).
Not suited to large groundwater seepage (p. 10-61).

sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility of soil nail walls (10.5.1.3.1 to 10.5.1.3.3).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of soil nail walls, 10.5.1.3.1 to 10.5.1.3.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 10-61)

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Soil nailing suits ground that stands unsupported 4 to 6 ft high for one to two days, nails above groundwater in permeable ground, and holes stable uncased. Well suited: dense granular soils with apparent cohesion, stiff fine-grained soils, engineered fill, residual soils, glacial till; marginal: non-engineered fill; unfavorable: dry clean sands, high groundwater, cobbles, soft clays, collapsible, organic, corrosive, karst, loess, expansive.
sections.body: Soil nail walls suit a wide range of ground and can be built in mixed stratigraphy if each layer is suitable and stable; unfavorable soils make them risky or costly. They are economical and feasible where the soil stands unsupported in a 4- to 6-foot ('6-fot', as printed) high near-vertical cut for one to two days (p. 10-62), nails in permeable ground are above the water table, and drill holes stay open uncased until grouted. Well suited: dense to very dense granular soils with apparent cohesion; weathered rock 'with adverse weakness planes' (as printed); stiff to hard fine-grained soils; engineered fill; residual soils; glacial till. Difficult or marginal: non-engineered fill; residual soils with unsuitable conditions. Unfavorable: dry, poorly graded cohesionless soils; granular soils with high groundwater; cobbles and boulders; soft to very soft fine-grained soils; collapsible soils; organic soils (p. 10-63); highly corrosive soil or groundwater; weathered rock with unfavorable weakness planes; karst; loess; glacial till (listed also as well suited, as printed); expansive soils. See GEC 7 for details. (pp. 10-61 to 10-63)
key_points: Soil must stand 4 to 6 ft unsupported for one to two days (p. 10-62).
Nails above the water table in permeable ground; holes stable uncased (p. 10-62).
Unfavorable: high groundwater, cobbles, soft clays, organics, karst, loess (p. 10-62).

sections.title: Environmental Considerations (GEC 7)
sections.summary: Corrosion potential must be evaluated on every soil nail project from pH, resistivity, chloride, sulfate and organic content; aggressive conditions (FHWA 2009) include acidic (pH < 5), sodic, calcareous and organic soils, industrial fills, coastal salts and deicing salts.
sections.body: Corrosion potential is of primary concern and must be evaluated on every project by laboratory tests of field samples and field tests of pH, electrical resistivity, chloride content, sulfate content and organic content. Factors making soils more aggressive (FHWA 2009): acidic soils (pH below 5; pyritic soils, soils high in soluble iron with acidic iron sulfides); sodic soils (western United States and arid areas); calcareous soils (alkaline, 7<pH<9, with sodium, calcium and calcium-magnesium carbonates and sulfates; mildly corrosive); organic soils (p. 10-64; anaerobic pockets with sulfate-reducing bacteria and severe pitting; peats, mucks, cinder, bogs, humic acid); industrial fills (slag, fly ash, construction debris, acid mine tailings); coastal salts; and road deicing salts in northern states. (pp. 10-63 to 10-64)
key_points: Evaluate corrosion on every project: pH, resistivity, chloride, sulfate, organics (p. 10-63).
Acidic soils pH < 5; calcareous 7 < pH < 9 (p. 10-63).
Organic soils risk sulfate-reducing bacteria and pitting (p. 10-64).

sections.body: Site conditions to consider in feasibility evaluation are listed in Section 5.3.1 Design Consideration and in Table 10-14 Initial Design Steps and Considerations. (p. 10-64)

sections.title: Alternative Solutions
sections.summary: Top-down alternatives to soil nail walls: ground anchored walls with flexible or stiff facing, sheetpile with or without deadman tiebacks, soldier pile and lagging, braced, soil mixing and jet grouted walls (FHWA 2008b); with room for a temporary backcut, bottom-up walls such as cantilever, gravity or MSE may be cheaper (p. 10-64).
sections.body: In cut situations where top-down construction will be used, alternative wall types are ground anchored walls with flexible or stiff facing, sheetpile with or without deadman tiebacks, soldier pile and lagging, braced, soil mixing and jet grouted wall structures (p. 10-64). See FHWA (2008b) for these systems and wall type selection guidance. If right-of-way and soil conditions are sufficient for a temporary backcut, bottom-up walls may be more economical than soil nail walls, including cantilever, gravity, semi gravity, counterfort concrete and MSE walls.
key_points: Top-down alternatives: anchored, sheetpile, soldier pile and lagging, braced, soil mix, jet grout walls.
Bottom-up walls may be cheaper if a temporary backcut is possible.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: General construction requirements for soil nail walls are in GEC 7; the section gives the general construction sequence, notes that walls may be specified by performance (end-result) or procedural (method) specifications, and describes materials in Section 5.2.2 (p. 10-64).
sections.body: General construction requirements and guidance for soil nail walls are in GEC 7 (p. 10-64). The general construction sequence is presented in Section 5.2.1. As discussed in Section 5.4, soil nail walls may be specified with a performance (end-result) or a procedural (method) specification. The variety of materials used are discussed in Section 5.2.2.
key_points: Guidance: GEC 7.
Specification may be end-result or method type.
sections.applicability: Entry point for soil nail wall construction sequence and materials.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Soil nail construction sequence (Figure 10-13): excavation lift typically 3 to 5 ft (2.5 to 7 ft) standing one to two days; drill; install and tremie-grout tendons and strip drains; 4-in. lightly reinforced initial shotcrete with bearing plate and nut tightened within 24 h, 72 h cure; repeat; final facing and drainage (pp. 10-65 to 10-67).
sections.body: The typical sequence (GEC 7; Figure 10-13, pp. 10-65 to 10-67): Step 1, excavation: the initial lift (unsupported cut) may range from 2.5 to 7 feet but is typically 3 to 5 feet, reaching slightly below the first nail row; the face must stand unsupported until nails and initial face are installed, typically one to two days, and the platform must be wide enough for the equipment. Step 2, drilling of nail holes from the platform, typically unsupported. Step 3A, nail installation and grouting: tendons placed with a tremie grout pipe and the hole filled under gravity or nominal low pressure; with hollow bars drilling and grouting are one operation. Step 3B, strip drains installed continuously on the face between nails and unrolled to the next lift. Step 4, initial shotcrete facing: typically a lightly reinforced 4-inch layer with WWM in the middle and bars around nail heads; a bearing plate is pressed into fresh shotcrete and the hex nut is wrench-tightened within 24 hours; some nails may be tested before the next lift; shotcrete must reach its 3-day strength before further excavation, with 72 hours assumed for planning. Step 5, subsequent levels repeat Steps 1-4, overlapping WWM by at least one full mesh cell. Step 6, final facing of CIP concrete, reinforced shotcrete or prefabricated panels, with weepholes, foot drain and ditches. Variations include shotcreting each lift before drilling where face stability is a concern, and placing the tendon in pre-grouted holes.
key_points: Excavation lift 2.5 to 7 ft, typically 3 to 5 ft; must stand one to two days.
Initial facing: lightly reinforced 4-in. shotcrete; nut tightened within 24 h.
Shotcrete 3-day strength before next lift; plan on 72 h cure.
WWM panels overlap at least one full mesh cell.

sections.summary: Main components of a solid bar soil nail wall (Figure 10-14); GEC 7 covers them in detail and gives guidance on hollow bar soil nail (HBSN) tendons (10.5.2.2.1 to 10.5.2.2.7).
sections.body: The main components of soil nail walls with a solid bar tendon are shown in Figure 10-14 and described in 10.5.2.2.1 to 10.5.2.2.7; GEC 7 gives detailed discussion and guidance on hollow bar soil nail (HBSN) tendons. (p. 10-67)
