sections.title: Tendons
sections.summary: Solid bars are the most common nails, set in typically 4 to 8 in. holes drilled usually 15 degrees below horizontal and grouted in two steps; threaded Grade 60 or 75 bars, commonly Nos. 8 to 11, up to 60 ft long, generally without splices or welds (GEC 7).
sections.body: Solid bar soil nails are the most commonly used, available in many sizes, thread types, steel grades and corrosion protection schemes. They go in typically 4- to 8-inch drill holes in a two-step operation: holes drilled at a shallow angle (usually 15 degrees from horizontal) by cased or open-hole methods (p. 10-68), then tendons inserted and grouted. Tendons are threaded, generally 60 ksi (Grade 60) or 75 ksi (Grade 75), commonly sizes Nos. 8, 9, 10 and 11; threaded bars are made up to 60 feet long, and tendons are generally continuous without splices or welds (GEC 7). (pp. 10-67 to 10-68)
key_points: Holes typically 4 to 8 in., usually 15 degrees below horizontal (p. 10-67).
Grade 60 or 75 threaded bars, Nos. 8 to 11, up to 60 ft (p. 10-68).
sections.applicability: Use when specifying soil nail tendons, hardware, grout, corrosion protection, facing and drainage.

sections.title: Connection Components
sections.summary: Bearing plate, beveled washers, hex nuts and washers connect the nail to the initial facing, headed studs to the final facing; plates are Grade 36 or 50 steel, usually square, 8 to 10 in. sides, 0.75 to 1 in. thick (GEC 7).
sections.body: The connection consists of bearing plates, beveled washers, hexagonal nuts, washers and headed studs: plate, nuts and washers connect the nail to the initial facing, headed studs connect it to the final facing. The bearing plate spreads the nail-end force onto the initial shotcrete and soil behind; it is commonly Grade 36 (AASHTO M183/ASTM A36) or Grade 50 steel, usually square and flat, 8 to 10 inches on a side and 0.75 to 1 inch thick (GEC 7). (p. 10-68)
key_points: Bearing plate Grade 36 or 50, 8-10 in. square, 0.75-1 in. thick (p. 10-68).
sections.applicability: Use when specifying soil nail tendons, hardware, grout, corrosion protection, facing and drainage.

sections.title: Grout
sections.summary: Neat cement grout fills the hole annulus, pumped by tremie soon after the bar is placed; the unfilled 'bird's beak' at the hole mouth is packed with shotcrete (GEC 7).
sections.body: Grout, generally neat cement, fills the annulus between tendon and soil; it is pumped shortly after the solid bar is placed, to limit squeezing or caving, by tremie through a grout tube. Because the hole is inclined, fresh grout cannot fill above the bottom of the hole opening; this 'bird's beak' is filled with shotcrete by hand-packing or during facing placement (GEC 7). (p. 10-68)
key_points: Neat cement grout by tremie soon after bar placement (p. 10-68).
Bird's beak filled with shotcrete (p. 10-68).
sections.applicability: Use when specifying soil nail tendons, hardware, grout, corrosion protection, facing and drainage.

sections.title: Centralizers
sections.summary: PVC or other non-corrosive centralizers fixed at regular intervals ensure minimum grout cover on the bar (GEC 7).
sections.body: Centralizers are installed at regular intervals along each solid bar so that a minimum grout thickness covers the tendon; they are securely attached and generally PVC or other non-corrosive synthetic material (GEC 7). (p. 10-68)
key_points: Centralizers ensure minimum grout cover (p. 10-68).
sections.applicability: Use when specifying soil nail tendons, hardware, grout, corrosion protection, facing and drainage.

sections.title: Corrosion Protection Elements
sections.summary: Beyond grout, bars can be encapsulated in corrugated HDPE or PVC sheaths (pre-grouted, annulus tremie grouted), fusion-bonded epoxy coated, or hot-dip galvanized with their hardware.
sections.body: Other devices add corrosion protection as needed. The bar can be encapsulated in corrugated high-density polyethylene (HDPE) or PVC sheath; sheathed, grouted bars are pre-manufactured (p. 10-69), and the annulus between sheath and hole is tremie grouted. Bars can be coated with fusion-bonded epoxy, a dielectric that impedes current, or bars and hardware hot-dip galvanized as sacrificial protection (after GEC 7). (pp. 10-68 to 10-69)
key_points: Encapsulation in corrugated HDPE or PVC sheath (p. 10-68).
Fusion-bonded epoxy or hot-dip galvanizing (p. 10-69).
sections.applicability: Use when specifying soil nail tendons, hardware, grout, corrosion protection, facing and drainage.

sections.title: Wall Facings
sections.summary: Permanent walls have an initial facing (shotcrete, welded wire mesh, waler and vertical bars at nail heads) supporting the soil during excavation, and a final facing of cast-in-place concrete or reinforced shotcrete for long-term resistance and finish.
sections.body: Permanent facings usually comprise an initial and a final facing. The initial facing, shotcrete with welded wire mesh and short waler and vertical bars around the nail heads, supports the soil between nails during excavation, connects the nails and protects the face from erosion and sloughing. The final facing, usually cast-in-place reinforced concrete or reinforced shotcrete, provides long-term structural resistance and the finish; GEC 7 covers plain and sculpted shotcrete, cast-in-place and precast panel facings. (p. 10-69)
key_points: Initial shotcrete facing plus final cast-in-place or shotcrete facing (p. 10-69).
sections.applicability: Use when specifying soil nail tendons, hardware, grout, corrosion protection, facing and drainage.

sections.title: Drainage
sections.summary: Vertical geocomposite strip drains behind the initial facing relieve water pressure, discharging to pipes or weepholes, but intercept water above the wall base, so with groundwater above the base design for hydrostatic pressure or install dewatering (e.g., horizontal drains); use a flow net for high groundwater.
sections.body: Geocomposite strip drains (core with a filter geotextile) are installed vertically behind the initial facing to eliminate or minimize water pressure on the face, with fittings discharging to a pipe drain and/or weepholes. They will likely not eliminate hydrostatic pressure from groundwater, since they intercept flow above the base of the wall; if groundwater is above the base, the wall must be designed for hydrostatic pressure or a dewatering system (e.g., horizontal drains) installed, and for high groundwater a flow net should be developed. (p. 10-69)
key_points: Strip drains do not eliminate hydrostatic pressure from groundwater (p. 10-69).
Groundwater above the base: design for it or dewater (p. 10-69).
sections.applicability: Use when specifying soil nail tendons, hardware, grout, corrosion protection, facing and drainage.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: GEC 7 soil nail design uses ASD and limit equilibrium slope stability to find nominal nail and component loads and slip surfaces, then LRFD checks for service, strength and extreme-event limit states consistent with AASHTO (2014), using GEC 7 resistance factors with AASHTO load factors (pp. 10-69 to 10-70).
sections.body: The soil nail wall design in GEC 7 relies on ASD- and limit equilibrium-based slope stability calculations to quantify nominal soil nail and component loads and the corresponding slip surface geometries (pp. 10-69 to 10-70). Those nominal loads are then used to perform LRFD checks. The GEC 7 LRFD framework considers service, strength and extreme-event limit states, consistent with AASHTO (2014). Recommended resistance factors for soil nail walls are in GEC 7, to be used with load factors in AASHTO (2014).
key_points: Nominal loads from ASD limit equilibrium; then LRFD checks.
Resistance factors from GEC 7; load factors from AASHTO (2014).
sections.applicability: Applies to the design framework for soil nail walls.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Project-specific requirements affecting soil nail wall design: wall height, length and location; physical constraints; effects on movement-sensitive adjacent structures; access and ROW; overhead and lateral limits; utilities; aesthetics; traffic closure; staging areas. A field reconnaissance is highly recommended (p. 10-70).
sections.body: Engineers must become familiar with the project-specific requirements that would affect the design, construction and performance of a soil nail wall (p. 10-70): preliminary site development plans with wall height, length and location relative to new infrastructure; physical constraints (wall near a bridge abutment, cut in steep terrain, near a waterway or subject to scour); potential effects on existing or future adjacent structures sensitive to movement; accessibility and right-of-way; overhead and lateral limitations; existing or new utilities in front of, under and behind the wall; aesthetics of the finish; need for partial or full traffic closure; and availability of staging areas. These are not unique to soil nail walls but must be carefully considered at the initial design stage, and a field reconnaissance is highly recommended (GEC 7).
key_points: Consider movement-sensitive adjacent structures and utilities early.
Field reconnaissance highly recommended.
sections.applicability: Use when gathering project requirements for soil nail wall design.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Tables 10-14 and 10-15 list soil nail wall design steps (GEC 7): project requirements, subsurface exploration and parameters, loads; then nail configuration, resistance factors, overall stability, strength limit states (pullout, tensile, facing), service limit states, seismic design, drainage, other considerations and drawings (pp. 10-70 to 10-72).
sections.body: The major steps and sub-steps are listed in Tables 10-14 and 10-15 (pp. 10-71 to 10-72, source GEC 7); the design requirements, guidance and example calculations are in GEC 7 (p. 10-70). Table 10-14, initial steps: Step 1, project requirements (requirements, standards and constraints; performance; preliminary geotechnical information); Step 2, subsurface exploration and design parameters (exploration, laboratory testing, soil corrosion potential and level of protection, profiles, soil parameters, seismic parameters, risk analysis); Step 3, load definition (unfactored service loads; load combinations and load factors). Table 10-15, main steps: Step 4, soil nail configuration and material selection (layout, cross sections, nail pattern, horizontal splaying, corrosion protection, nail type and properties); Step 5, selection of resistance factors; Step 6, overall stability (internal, global, basal heave and sliding if applicable); Step 7, strength limit states (pullout, sliding, nail tensile resistance, facing flexural, punching shear and headed stud resistance, other facing considerations); Step 8, service limit states (lateral and vertical displacements; lateral squeeze if applicable); Step 9, seismic design (parameters, adjusted coefficients, overall stability with seismic loads); Step 10, drainage (internal, surface runoff, details, specialty items); Step 11, other considerations (constructability, load-testing and monitoring plans); Step 12, construction drawings and specifications.
key_points: Initial steps 1-3: requirements, exploration and parameters, loads (Table 10-14).
Main steps 4-12: configuration, resistance factors, stability, strength and service limit states, seismic, drainage, drawings (Table 10-15).
Strength checks: pullout, nail tension, facing flexure, punching shear, headed studs.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: The primary reference for soil nail wall design is GEC 7 (2015), Soil Nail Walls Reference Manual (FHWA NHI-14-007); AASHTO (2014) does not address soil nail walls; FHWA (1994) Soil Nailing Field Inspectors Manual gives greater detail on inspection and testing (pp. 10-72 to 10-73).
sections.body: The primary reference for design of soil nail walls for transportation works is GEC 7 (2015), Soil Nail Walls Reference Manual (Lazarte et al.; FHWA NHI-14-007) (p. 10-72). The current AASHTO (2014) specifications do not address soil nail walls, though they are expected to be included in future updates. Installation and construction procedures are integral to the design process; GEC 7 discusses construction quality assurance, and greater detail on inspection methods, nail testing, inspection forms and difficult ground during construction is in FHWA (1994), Soil Nailing Field Inspectors Manual (Porterfield, Cotton and Byrne; FHWA-SA-93-068) (p. 10-73).
key_points: Primary: GEC 7 (2015).
AASHTO (2014) does not address soil nail walls.
Inspection detail: FHWA (1994).

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Heading for soil nail wall construction specifications and quality assurance: specification development, quality assurance with Table 10-16 inspector responsibilities and nail load testing, and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (pp. 10-73 to 10-78).
sections.body: Section 5.4 (p. 10-73) gives an overview of soil nail wall construction specifications and quality assurance: specification development (5.4.1), quality assurance including inspector responsibilities and verification and proof testing (5.4.2), and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (5.4.3).
sections.applicability: Entry point for contracting, inspection and monitoring of soil nail walls.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Permanent soil nail walls are contracted by a procedural (method) approach with all design, materials and methods specified, or a performance (end-result) approach with outcome criteria and a contractor design submittal; selection depends on criticality, complexity, owner experience and contractor availability (p. 10-73).
sections.body: Two contracting methods can be used for permanent soil nail walls (p. 10-73): a procedural or method approach, with all details of design, construction materials and methods specified in the contract documents; and a performance or end-result approach, where the documents specify criteria for a successful outcome without prescribing full design, detailing or methods, and a detailed design submittal accompanies the construction drawings. Both are valid if properly implemented, each with advantages and potential disadvantages. The method is selected based on the criticality and complexity of the project, the experience of the owner and its consultants, and the availability of specialty contractors. See GEC 7 and/or GeoTechTools for specification guidance and examples.
key_points: Method (procedural) or end-result (performance) contracting.
Choice depends on criticality, complexity, owner experience and contractor availability.
sections.applicability: Applies to choosing a contracting method for permanent soil nail walls.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Soil nail QA covers material and activity inspection, identifying conditions needing changed procedures or design, and nail load testing. Steel accepted by mill certificates plus visual checks; Table 10-16 lists inspector duties by phase; verification tests and proof tests on at least 5 percent of production nails (pp. 10-73 to 10-78).
sections.body: Construction QA includes inspection of materials, inspection of construction activities, identification of site or soil conditions requiring modified procedures or design, and load testing of installed nails (p. 10-73). Material inspection covers quality, storage and corrosion protection (p. 10-74). Steel components (tendons, plates, nuts, washers, WWM, rebar) are normally accepted on mill certifications plus visual inspection for transport or storage damage; cement on producer certification pending grout compressive tests; potable water is generally suitable without testing; corrosion protection of all tendons is inspected on site, and damaged protection is repaired or the tendon replaced. Table 10-16 (pp. 10-74 to 10-77, source FHWA 2008b) lists inspector responsibilities by phase: contractor set up; nail storage and handling (keep dry, off the ground); excavation (line and grade, soil identification, face stability, no over-excavation, sequencing, seepage); drilling (method suited to ground, tolerances, hard drilling, no loss of ground); tendon installation and grouting (hole condition, bar and coating damage, grout volume, minimum length, centralizers, tremie from the bottom, no auger reversal); load testing (calibration, gauges, cure time, retest only after procedures are modified); drainage installation; wall facing (mix, reinforcement position, thickness, joints, test panels); and post installation (pay quantities). Both contractor and inspector should understand the soil conditions assumed in design (pp. 10-77 to 10-78). Verification tests confirm that the contractor's methods achieve the design pullout resistance and bond strength; proof tests, generally on a minimum of 5 percent of production nails, verify there are no significant variations across the wall.
key_points: Steel accepted on mill certificates plus visual inspection.
Grout placed by tremie from the bottom of the hole, pipe kept below the grout level.
Proof tests on a minimum of 5 percent of production nails; verification tests confirm design bond.
Do not retest a failed nail until installation procedures are modified.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Soil nail wall monitoring may use inclinometers, survey points, load cells and strain gauges; it should be included for critical or unusual walls, for at least 1 year after construction, with each instrument selected to answer a specific question (p. 10-78).
sections.body: Performance monitoring instrumentation for soil nail walls could include inclinometers, wall survey points, load cells and/or strain gauges (p. 10-78). Inclinometers and survey points measure wall movements during and after construction; strain gauges measure the development and distribution of nail forces to improve future designs. Performance monitoring should be included in any critical or unusual soil nail wall installation, and monitoring for at least 1 year after construction is recommended to examine service deformation and stress development in the nails and facing as a function of load, time and environmental changes such as freeze-thaw cycles (GEC 7). If a monitoring program is used, first define the purpose of the measurements; every instrument should be selected and placed to answer a specific question, and if there is no question there should be no instrumentation.
key_points: Instruments: inclinometers, survey points, load cells, strain gauges.
Monitor critical or unusual walls for at least 1 year after construction.
sections.applicability: Applies to performance monitoring of soil nail walls.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Permanent soil nail walls on public transportation projects typically cost about $70 to $100 per square foot of wall (2014) and can save 10 to 30 percent compared with other common retaining structures when conventional procedures are used (pp. 10-78 to 10-79).
sections.body: The construction costs of permanent soil nail walls in public transportation projects typically range from approximately $70 to $100 per square foot of wall in 2014 (p. 10-78). Compared with typical cost ranges for other commonly used retaining structures on highway projects, soil nail walls can provide a 10 to 30 percent cost savings when conventional soil nailing construction procedures are used (pp. 10-78 to 10-79). Actual construction cost may be considerably lower or higher depending on the factors listed in Section 5.5.1 (GEC 7).
key_points: Typical permanent wall cost about $70 to $100 per square foot (2014).
10 to 30 percent savings versus other common retaining structures.
sections.applicability: Use for preliminary cost comparison of soil nail walls.

sections.title: Factors Affecting Cost and Construction Schedule
sections.summary: Factors affecting soil nail wall cost and schedule: specialty contractor availability, mobilization, access and ROW, working space and drill platform, variable ground, temporary face support or berms, drilling obstructions, casing needs, facing aesthetics, seismicity and frost, and extra verification tests (p. 10-79).
sections.body: Important factors in cost comparison for soil nail walls (p. 10-79; see GEC 7 for more) are: availability of specialty contractors skilled in soil nailing and shotcrete near the site; cost of mobilization; site accessibility and right-of-way; sufficient space to operate equipment, including a drill platform; large variations of ground conditions over small distances, requiring frequent changes of drilling equipment and procedures; need for temporary support of exposed soil between lifts, including an intermediate soil berm; difficult drilling due to obstructions (utilities, large aggregate or stone particles); need for in-hole stability such as casing to avoid collapse; special facing aesthetics such as precast panels or sculpted facings; regional conditions including high seismicity and frost susceptibility; and changing ground conditions requiring numerous additional verification load tests.
key_points: Contractor availability, mobilization, access and working space.
Variable ground, obstructions, casing, temporary face support.
Aesthetic facings, seismicity, frost, extra verification tests.
sections.applicability: Applies to estimating cost and schedule risk for soil nail walls.

sections.title: Related and Alternative Technologies
sections.summary: Section heading for technologies related to the four primary reinforcement applications: deep patching, shored MSE walls, stable feature MSE walls, shoot-in nails, screw-in nails and construction working platforms (pp. 10-80 to 10-84).
sections.body: Section 6.0 (p. 10-80) describes related and alternative reinforced soil technologies: deep patching (6.1), shored MSE walls for steep terrain and low volume roads (6.2), stable feature MSE walls (6.3), shoot-in nails (6.4), screw-in nails (6.5) and construction working platforms (6.6).
sections.applicability: Entry point for reinforced soil technologies beyond the four primary applications.

sections.title: Deep Patching
sections.summary: Deep patch is a temporary mitigation for sliding road sections in steep terrain, usually side-cast fills: layers of soil reinforcement in the top of the failing embankment, built from the road by a small crew; it slows rather than stops movement; empirical design in Musser and Denning (2005), reviewed in FHWA (2012) (p. 10-80).
sections.body: The deep patch is a temporary mitigation technique for sliding roadway sections in steep terrain, typically on roads with chronic slide movements resulting mainly from side cast fill construction (p. 10-80). A main advantage is that it is built with equipment operating from the roadway, without accessing the toe of the failed area. It is generally not expected to completely arrest movement but to slow it to manageable levels. Deep patch repairs reinforce the top of a failing embankment with several layers of soil reinforcement (Figure 10-15). The work is typically done by a small crew of a laborer, hydraulic excavator and dump truck. Design determines the extent of the roadway failure from visual observations of cracking and then uses analytical or empirical methods for the reinforcement requirements. An empirical design procedure is in the Deep Patch Road Embankment Repair Application Guide (Musser and Denning 2005, USDA Forest Service with FHWA Federal Lands), and a review of the design methodology is in FHWA (2012).
key_points: Temporary repair; slows rather than arrests movement.
Built from the roadway without toe access.
Empirical design: Musser and Denning (2005); review: FHWA (2012).
figures: Figure 10-15: Deep patch roadway embankment repair. (Musser and Denning 2005; p. 10-80)
sections.applicability: Applies to temporary repair of chronically sliding roadway fills in steep terrain.

sections.title: Shored MSE Walls for Steep Terrains and Low Volume Roads
sections.summary: In steep terrain MSE walls need benches for reinforcement longer than 8 ft or 70% of wall height; where excavation is impractical, shoring (usually soil nail walls) stabilizes the back-cut with an MSE wall in front, forming a shored MSE (SMSE) wall that can reduce long-term pressures (FHWA 2006; GEC 11) (p. 10-81).
sections.body: In steep terrain, MSE wall construction requires excavation for a flat bench to accommodate reinforcements with a minimum length of greater than 8 feet or 70 percent of the wall height, and the required embedment is proportional to the steepness of the slope below the toe (p. 10-81). In some cases the excavation becomes substantial and unshored excavation is impractical, particularly where traffic must be maintained. Shoring, most often soil nail walls, has been used to stabilize the backslope (back-cut), with an MSE wall designed and built in front of it (Figure 10-16). If the shoring wall is designed as permanent, it can significantly reduce the long-term lateral pressures on the MSE wall. This configuration is a shored MSE (SMSE) wall; details are in FHWA (2006), with additional design and detailing guidance in GEC 11.
key_points: MSE reinforcement minimum length greater than 8 ft or 70% of wall height.
Shoring usually soil nail walls; permanent shoring reduces long-term pressure on the MSE wall.
Guidance: FHWA (2006) and GEC 11.
figures: Figure 10-16: Generic cross-section of a shored MSE (SMSE) wall system for steep terrains. (FHWA 2006; p. 10-81)
sections.applicability: Applies to MSE walls for widening low volume roads in steep terrain with limited excavation.

sections.title: Stable Feature (SFMSE) MSE Walls
sections.summary: MSE walls may be built in front of apparently stable features such as a rock face; depending on the space between wall face and feature, a stable feature MSE (SFMSE) wall may behave like an SMSE wall; guidelines and minimum geometry are in GEC 11 (p. 10-82).
sections.body: MSE walls can be considered in front of apparently stable features such as a rock face, as shown in Figure 10-17 (p. 10-82). Depending on the space between the MSE wall face and the stable feature, the behavior of the stable feature MSE (SFMSE) wall may be similar to that of a shored MSE (SMSE) wall. Guidelines for designing and detailing such cases are summarized in GEC 11; Figure 10-17 shows the minimum recommended geometry of an SFMSE wall system.
key_points: SFMSE walls are built in front of stable features such as rock faces.
Behavior may resemble SMSE walls depending on the gap; guidance in GEC 11.
figures: Figure 10-17: Minimum recommended geometry of a stable feature MSE (SFMSE) wall system. (GEC 11; p. 10-82)
sections.applicability: Applies to MSE walls constructed close in front of rock faces or other stable features.

sections.title: Shoot-In Nails
sections.summary: Shoot-in nails are launched at over 200 mph at pressures approaching 2,500 psi to build temporary nail walls; bars typically 1-1/2 in. in diameter and up to 20 ft long act as dowels in shear and bending, not as drilled and grouted soil nails; proprietary with limited design procedures (pp. 10-82 to 10-83).
sections.body: Shoot-in nails use a high pressure system to insert passive inclusions into the ground to construct a temporary soil nail wall (p. 10-82). The bars are launched into the soil at high speeds over 200 miles per hour at pressures approaching 2,500 psi. Bars can be perforated fiberglass, perforated galvanized steel tube or bare steel tubes, typically 1-1/2 inches in diameter and up to 20 feet long. An epoxy-coated small-diameter threaded bar can be inserted into the tube after pressure grouting to increase structural capacity. Installation is fast with little site impact, but nail penetration length may be hard to control. Advantages include rapid construction, easy monitoring and testing, limited headroom and right-of-way, and tolerance of large deformations; potential disadvantages are that it is a proprietary, licensed technology, needs specialized contractors and equipment, and lacks simple, comprehensive design procedures. Applications include landslide repair and roadway and embankment widening (p. 10-83). Because the bars are generally not drilled and grouted, they do not meet the GEC 7 definition of a soil nail; a shoot-in nail acts as a dowel, contributing mainly through shear and localized bending, with limited axial capacity without grout. See GeoTechTools, USDA (1994a, 1994b) and Malouf and Collin (2013).
key_points: Launch speed over 200 mph at pressures approaching 2,500 psi.
Bars typically 1-1/2 in. diameter, up to 20 ft long.
Act as dowels (shear and bending), not as drilled and grouted nails.
Proprietary; lacks simple comprehensive design procedures.
sections.applicability: Applies to temporary nail walls, landslide repairs and widening using launched nails.

sections.title: Screw-In Nails
sections.summary: Screw-in (helical) soil nails are 1.5-in. square steel shafts with welded helices spaced about 3.6 times the helix diameter, installed by torque; they act as anchors by helix bearing, not as grouted soil nails; used where access is difficult or areas small; corrosion is the major concern (pp. 10-83 to 10-84).
sections.body: Screw-in soil nailing uses helical soil nails to stabilize retained soils (p. 10-83). The nails typically comprise a 1.5-inch square solid steel shaft with steel helices welded at regular intervals, installed with drilling equipment of sufficient torque to penetrate the native soils. Helix spacing is a function of helix diameter, typically about 3.6 times the diameter. Screw-in nails are typically used in places difficult to access or for small areas (Collin and Cowell 1998). The bars are not drilled and grouted and so do not meet the GEC 7 definition of a soil nail; a screw-in nail acts as an anchor, contributing to stability by bearing resistance of the helices rather than by bond stress along the reinforcement (pp. 10-83 to 10-84). The installation is shown in Figure 10-19. The major concern is corrosion, because galvanization and coatings are damaged during installation, increasing exposure. Detailed information is at GeoTechTools (GEC 7).
key_points: Shaft typically 1.5-in. square solid steel; helix spacing about 3.6 times helix diameter.
Acts as an anchor by helix bearing, not by grout bond.
Corrosion is the major concern because coatings are damaged during installation.
sections.applicability: Applies to helical nail stabilization at small or hard-to-access sites.

sections.title: Construction Working Platform
sections.summary: Construction working platforms use geosynthetic reinforcement in granular fill to support equipment and traffic over soft soils without mud waves or excessive ruts; design is based on local bearing capacity (with reinforced Nc values, Chapter 9) or slope stability, and is often done by the contractor (p. 10-84).
sections.body: Construction working platforms use geosynthetic reinforcement in granular fill to form a temporary platform that supports construction equipment and traffic over soft soils, avoiding mud waves and excessive ruts (p. 10-84). The geosynthetic layer increases the local bearing resistance of the soft subgrade. Design is commonly based on local bearing capacity or on slope stability; researchers have suggested different bearing capacity factors, Nc, for unreinforced versus geotextile-reinforced and geogrid-reinforced unpaved platforms, as covered in Chapter 9. A single geosynthetic layer is commonly used. Many ground modification techniques require heavy equipment on the soft soils to be modified, and contractors often use a working platform for temporary access and support, so platform design is often performed by the contractor.
key_points: Geosynthetic in granular fill increases local bearing resistance of soft subgrade.
Design by local bearing capacity (reinforced Nc, Chapter 9) or slope stability.
Usually a single layer; often designed by the contractor.
sections.applicability: Applies to temporary equipment platforms over soft ground for ground modification work.
